title: Who Dat
logline: Super Bowl Sunday on Dupre Street: the eight o’clock Mass in a family’s pew, a phone that rings at the kickoff, a kick nobody in the room can watch, and a city that has waited forty-three seasons to go outside.

s01.slug: SUNDAY · 6:40 AM · N. DUPRE STREET, THE ATTIC → THE FRONT ROOM
body: The light gets into the attic gray, through the gable window and the blades of the box fan, which chop it on the way in and lay it across the mattresses in slats. Over Jack’s face the nails come down through the roof deck in rows, an inch of point apiece, and every point holds its own bead of cold. The fan is still on the louder of its two settings. It pulls Dupre Street in over him a piece at a time: a dog two yards down, a screen door on a spring, a car that won’t turn over and then does.

By the hatch, Kevin’s sleeping bag is rolled tight and squared to the edge of the boards, with his pillow set square on top of it. Theo is asleep on the middle mattress with his mouth open and one arm off the side, knuckles on the floor, in a T-shirt that cost more than the fan.
Margot has the Gideon downstairs. Jack lies on his back under Remy’s Tiger and says the penance from memory, lips moving, the sound kept down in his chest.

*He summoned the Twelve and began to send them out two by two.* The rafters over him are rough-sawn and dark with old heat. *He instructed them to take nothing for the journey but a walking stick* — no bread, no bag, no money in their belts. *They were, however, to wear sandals but not a second tunic.*

The next verse is right behind it. *Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave from there.* The rest comes after it in order, the dust shaken off the feet at the door of any place that won’t have them, the oil, the sick made well, and he says it through to the last word and lies there under the nails with the fan going.
Under the mattress the house creaks once, somewhere down in the walls, and settles.

The attic stairs are closer to a ladder than to stairs, and he takes them backward in his socks with his boots in one hand. At the foot of them, in the front room, Mémère is in her armchair with the lamp on and her beads going, dressed for the eight o’clock at a quarter to seven: a black dress, a black cardigan buttoned to the collar, a small black hat with a long pin run through it, and on the cardigan a gold fleur-de-lis no bigger than a thumbnail. Behind her the daybed is made up tight, the spread turned square under the pillow, and the big television across the room is dark, with a fistful of Carnival throws, gold and purple, hung over one corner of it. The beads in her hand stop.
“*Bon.*” They start again under her thumb. “Two of you are up. The other sleeps like a Protestant.”

Past her shoulder, through the front window, Dupre Street is gray and shut, with every porch light on the block still burning, and the Odyssey sits at the curb with its back glass to the house. WHO DAT · 1 DAYS, in white, the way it came in from Texas. Somebody has drawn a 0 over the 1 in lipstick, a dark gold-brown, the stroke heavy where it started and thin where it closed. On the porch rail a lipstick tube stands on its end with the cap off.
“Coffee’s on the stove,” Mémère says. “Bring me one. Then you sit.”

The kitchen has only the light over the stove. The coffee is in an old drip pot on the back burner, the enamel chipped down to the iron at the spout, and when he tips it the chicory comes out black, smelling half of chocolate and half of something burnt on purpose. The cayenne tin stands next to the salt. On the parish calendar by the phone, St. Jude is still holding up January. He takes two cups off the drainboard, one from Broussard’s Seafood and one from a bank in Baton Rouge, and brings her the one without the chip.
She points hers at the end of the daybed. He sits on it, with his boots on the rug between his feet.
“What does your mama cook on Sunday?”
“Gravy. Sauce. My grandmother’s. At two o’clock.” At home it’s on the stove by nine, and Nonna stands over it from then till two with the wooden spoon and doesn’t sit down.
“*Bon.*” She drinks. “Your daddy goes to Mass?”
Jack looks into his cup. “Sometimes.”
“Sometimes is a lot of men.”

She says something to herself in French, short, with *maigre* in it, which he has heard about himself before, and a nod at the end, and doesn’t put it into English for him. He drinks his coffee. It’s the first hot thing he’s had since the gumbo, and he can feel exactly where it goes.
In the inside pocket of the Carhartt, against his ribs, the RAZR goes twice.

s02.slug: SUNDAY · 7:15 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — ONE BATHROOM
body: From the kitchen table, with his second cup of chicory, Jack listens to the house find its stairs. The attic hatch bangs back. The ladder takes somebody’s weight a rung at a time and complains about every one. Doors go all down the hall, Tess’s old room and Josie’s and the bathroom’s, and in the front room a lamp clicks off because the window has caught up with it.

Eleven people and one bathroom, not counting Mémère, who went through it before the sun was up and is in her chair with her hat on. Celeste runs the line from the middle of the hall in a whisper, a nurse’s station at shift change: “Remy, out. Margot, baby, you’re next. Theo, nobody needs that long.”

Margot does not go when she’s called. She stands in the kitchen door in black, sweater and skirt and tights, as always, with her notebook shut on one finger. “I’m attending as an observer,” she tells the hall.
From the front room, Mémère: “God observes. You can sit.”
Margot takes that under advisement and goes to stand outside the bathroom door with her toothbrush.

Laney comes up the hall behind her in one of Lena’s Mass dresses, navy with a white collar, a size wrong in every direction and magnificent anyway, and stops in the kitchen doorway to let the room look at it. Theo, coming out of the bathroom with a towel round his neck, opens his mouth. Laney points at him. He shuts it. “I am a *vision* in borrowed navy,” Laney says, “and I will be taking no questions at this time.”

Tony comes through from the front of the house in his Sunday sport coat, brown, with brass buttons, and under it, where a shirt and tie ought to be, a Brees jersey with the gold 9 showing in the V, put on under the coat with the care of a vestment. He kisses the top of Celeste’s head on his way past her in the hall, pours himself a coffee, sets it down on the counter to hunt for his reading glasses, and goes out the front without it. In a minute WWL comes back through two doors from the porch rail, a man talking very fast about Miami.

Jude is standing at the sink eating a cold boiled potato out of the colander from last night’s boil, skin and all, like an apple. Tess and Beau come in the back door from their place with Lucille asleep in a black-and-gold knit cap with a fleur-de-lis sewn on the top, and the baby goes from lap to lap down the table and doesn’t wake for any of them. Kevin comes in behind them from the back steps with his beads in his pocket and the boards of the steps still printed across the knees of his khakis, and says good morning to every person in the kitchen one at a time, by name, including Lucille.

And Lena is at the stove with her back to all of it, in a black dress with a dish towel tucked in at the waist, scrambling eggs for the house in Mémère’s iron skillet with a wooden spoon gone black at the business end. She salts, and stirs, and says “Plates” over her shoulder, and Josie brings plates.

Celeste comes through on her way to somewhere else and puts a loaf of bread in Jack’s hands without stopping. “Toast, baby. The broiler.” The broiler is the drawer at the bottom of the old Magic Chef, at Lena’s knees, and the sheet pan has to come out past her every time, so for ten minutes they work the one stove together. Her hip moves the skillet’s handle out of his road before he gets to it. He holds the drawer open with his foot so she can reach across it for the cayenne. She says “Butter,” and it’s in her hand. She doesn’t look at him and he doesn’t look at her, and the toast comes out right, three pans of it.
“Mama,” Remy says from the table, “you got him *working*?”
“He’s got hands,” Celeste whispers from the hall, and that’s the end of that. Jack puts the toast on the table and sits where she points.

body.text: At the table Theo has a cup of chicory and his chair tipped back. When Celeste asks after his mother he says she’s fine, she’s at a friend’s in Pasadena, and that’s all he says about it, and Jack watches him say it and drink his coffee after.
body.else: At the table Theo has a cup of chicory, his chair tipped back on two legs, and an audience. “My mother’s pool is now a pond,” he tells it. “A hill came down in the night. She’s at a friend’s in Pasadena with the dogs, and she would like everyone to know she’s *fine*.” He does *fine* in her voice, from a long way down a phone line, and gets the table, Kevin included. Tony is back in the doorway for the coffee he forgot. “Tell her we know about mud,” Tony says. “Then you stock it with redfish.” Theo tips his cup to him. “I’ll tell her you’re taking bids.” Tony goes back out to his radio with the cup this time, and Theo’s face, start to finish, is doing its very best work.

body: Kevin looks at the clock over the stove before he takes a piece of toast, out of habit, and does the sum for the table: Communion around twenty to nine, so they’re fine, an hour and change. “Kevin knows,” Mémère says from the front room, and that’s the canon law settled.

Josie is buttering toast at the counter with her weight on one hip, Lena’s hip, under Lena’s eyebrows, and when the noise has gone round once she points the butter knife across the kitchen at Jack and says, at the volume of a thirteen-year-old with information:

body.text: “Is your girlfriend in Canada watching the game?”
Remy, at the table with his fork up and waiting on eggs, is delighted. “Everybody’s got a girlfriend in Canada, Jo-Jo. I got two.”
body.else: Remy, at the table with his fork up and waiting on eggs, is delighted. “Everybody’s got a girlfriend somewhere, Jo-Jo. I got two.”

body: Laney looks at the ceiling. At the stove, Lena’s back doesn’t change. The spoon goes round the skillet, and round.

response: “I do, actually,” Jack says. “She’s working.”
“*Working*,” Remy says, and that finishes him. He has to hold the edge of the table. “Jo-Jo. She’s got a *job*.”
At the stove the flame goes off under the skillet. “She’s real, Remy,” Lena says, with her back to them. “Eat your eggs.”

She brings the skillet to the table and spoons eggs onto a plate and puts the plate in front of Remy, and spoons out another and puts that one in front of Jack, and takes the skillet back where it came from. What Jack gets of her is a black sleeve going by, and her shoulder, and the back of her neck where her hair is pinned up for church.

choices.text: “She’s cheering for the Colts. To keep it interesting.”
choices.key: At breakfast on Dupre Street Josie asked about your girlfriend, at full volume. You said she’s cheering for the Colts, to keep it interesting. Lena told Remy she’s real, and to eat his eggs.
response: “She’s cheering for the Colts,” Jack says. “To keep it interesting.”

“The *Colts*.” Remy has to put his fork down. He looks around the kitchen for somebody to share it with and settles on Beau, who is holding the baby and can’t get away. “He brought a Colts fan into this house. On *this* day.”

The skillet comes to the table. A plate goes down in front of Remy, and a plate goes down in front of Jack, and Lena’s arm is the only part of her in it. “She’s real, Remy,” she says from over his head. “Eat your eggs.”
Then she’s back at the stove, running water into the skillet so it hisses.

choices.text: “She’s real. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks. She’ll be watching.”

response: “She’s real,” Jack says. “She’s in Vancouver for two weeks. She’ll be watching.”
Remy is beside himself. “*Vancouver*,” he says. “Two *weeks*.” He looks to his sisters for help.
From the stove, a moment behind it, with her back to the table, Lena says, “She’s real, Remy. Eat your eggs.” She says it to Remy.

She comes with the skillet and puts a plate in front of her brother, and then one in front of Jack. The eggs have cayenne in them, and green onion cut fine, and she has gone back to the stove while he is still finding a word for that.

body: Celeste puts her head in from the hall. “Seven forty-five on the steps,” she whispers. “Mémère doesn’t wait and God doesn’t either.”
Jude puts the rest of his potato back in the colander, for later. Jack eats his eggs. In the front room Mémère is already working her gloves on, a finger at a time.

s03.slug: SUNDAY · 7:58 AM · OUR LADY OF THE HOLY ROSARY, ESPLANADE AVENUE — THE PEW
body: The eight o’clock is half full and dressed for two things. Sunday coats go over black and gold in every other pew. An usher at the back has a fleur-de-lis pin in his lapel, and the man beside him, waiting with the collection basket on its long handle, is wearing a Brees jersey under his windbreaker and is not hiding it. Two pews up a baby in a Saints bib is eating the bib. The doors are propped open behind them, and through them Esplanade is gray under its oaks, the neutral ground still wet, a woman in a gold sweatshirt walking a dog on it. The altar is dressed in green.

Inside the doors, at the font, Lena wets her fingers and holds them back over her shoulder to him, and he touches his own to them and crosses himself with her water, the way his mother does it for his father at the door of the church at home, the Sundays his father comes. Behind him he hears Laney stop walking.

The Broussards have two pews on the Gospel side, and Mémère has the aisle end of the first, where the kneeler’s leather is worn pale in two places the size of her knees. Celeste stands at the end of the pew and seats them with a touch between the shoulder blades, one at a time, in an order she must have settled on the walk over: Mémère; Jack; Lena; Laney; Theo. Behind them, Tony and herself, Remy, Josie, Jude, Tess, and Beau with Lucille, and at the far end Kevin and Margot. Jack is put between the grandmother and the granddaughter, and he sits where he’s put.

The bulletin is folded into the missalette in the rack in front of him, the parish name across the top in old church type and under it REV. LUCIEN HÉBERT, PASTOR. Lena tips her head toward him, eyes on the altar. “He baptized all six of us,” she says. “And Lucille, in January. In the third quarter.”
“Carolina?”
“Daddy had the radio in his coat.”

Behind him Tony goes down onto the kneeler like a toolbox set down hard, and before the procession has so much as moved he prays, aloud, loud enough for three pews: “Lord, I wore the bag for You. One and fifteen, I wore the bag. You owe me one.”
Celeste doesn’t look up from her missalette. Mémère doesn’t turn her head. “*Antoine.*”
Down the row Laney makes a sound into her hand and tries to turn it into a cough, and it fools nobody, and Lena’s elbow goes into her ribs without the rest of Lena moving at all.

The organ starts, and they stand. Father Hébert comes up the aisle behind a boy with the cross and two girls with candles: a small man in his seventies with the slight roll in his walk of somebody raised on a levee, in a green chasuble with a Saints pin on it over the heart, and nothing more than the pin. On his way past the Broussard pews he looks them over, both rows, end to end.
A lector in a black-and-gold scarf reads Isaiah: the seraph taking the ember from the altar with tongs and touching it to the prophet’s mouth, and the prophet answering, *Here I am; send me!*

The cantor gives them the psalm, *In the sight of the angels I will sing your praises, Lord*, and the pew sings it back: Mémère high and cracked and half a beat behind, Laney a beat late and game, Theo moving his mouth, and on Jack’s other side Lena, a third under the tune, finding a harmony of her own down there and staying in it. Jack loses his place in the verse twice.

The lector reads Paul, the risen Christ appearing to Cephas, then the Twelve, then more than five hundred at once, and *last of all, as to one born abnormally*, to Paul himself. On *abnormally*, two pews up, the baby gives the bib up and starts on its fist.

Hébert reads the Gospel himself. The crowd pressing on the shore of the lake; Jesus getting into Simon’s boat to have room to talk; then, to Simon, put out into deep water. *Master, we have worked hard all night and have caught nothing* — and Jack, one night out of thirty-five hours in a van, hears it go by — *but at your command I will lower the nets.* The nets fill until they tear. They wave in the other boat, and both boats fill until they start to go under, and Simon Peter falls at Jesus’s knees in among the fish. *Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.* Hébert reads it without leaning on it and lets it go up into the ceiling with the fans.
He closes the book and looks out at them with his hands on the ambo. “Half of you have pulled a net,” he says, in a voice with Mémère’s Breaux Bridge in it. “The other half married somebody who did.”
The church laughs, and Tony laughs loudest.

“Peter knows that lake,” Hébert says. “He knows you don’t catch nothing in deep water in the daytime. He tells the Lord so. And he lets the net down anyway, because somebody told him to.” Two pews up the baby says something, and he nods to it. “And when the boat’s going under with fish, Peter gets down in the fish and tells the Lord to go away. The Lord don’t go. He gives the man a job.” He looks down at the Broussard pews, and at the rest of the black and gold. “This evening some of you will ask God for things He has not promised. Ask Him anyway. And if He says no, the gumbo is still good.”
“*Amen*,” Tony says, a beat early, and the church laughs again, the laugh of people who have said it to each other in kitchens all week.

The Creed, the gifts going up the aisle, the basket on its long handle working down the rows, the Our Father, with Lena’s hand on the edge of the pew beside his and not touching it, from *Our Father* to *deliver us from evil*, where the priest takes it back.
At the sign of peace Mémère goes first: a dry hand, small and twice as strong as it looks, a squeeze, “*La paix.*” Then Lena, on his other side, holding hers out.

choices.text: “Peace be with you, Lena.”
choices.key: At the sign of peace at Holy Rosary, between Lena and her grandmother, you said: Peace be with you, Lena.
response: “Peace be with you, Lena.”
Her hand is warm from the pew and has the ridge of a pen callus on the middle finger, and she looks at him for the answer, not at the hand. “And also with you.”

She doesn’t let go. Around them the church is shaking hands across the pews and over the backs of them, and Lena keeps his hand until Laney leans across her with her own hand out, and only then gives it up, so that Laney can shake it, cool and correct, the handshake for a groomsman she has been warned about. Up at the altar Hébert breaks the host, and the organ starts the Lamb of God.

choices.text: *Just take her hand.*
choices.key: At the sign of peace at Holy Rosary you took Lena’s hand and didn’t say anything. Neither did she.
response: He takes it, and says nothing, and she says nothing back.

Her hand is warm from the pew. It goes on as long as a handshake can before it has to be called something else, with the church murmuring *peace* all round them in a hundred voices, and it is the organ starting the Lamb of God that ends it, and Laney’s hand coming across Lena’s lap for his, cool and correct.
Lena puts her hand back in her lap, and lays the other one over it.

choices.text: “Peace be with you, Navigator.”
choices.key: At the sign of peace at Holy Rosary you said: Peace be with you, Navigator. And also with you, Youngstown.
response: “Peace be with you, Navigator.”
Her mouth goes. She gets it back. “And also with you, Youngstown.”

On his other side Mémère hears *Youngstown* and looks at the altar very hard. Laney is already reaching across Lena for him, her hand out, cool and correct, and while he’s still shaking it the organ comes in under them with the Lamb of God. At the far end of the row Theo is looking up at the ceiling fans as if he’s been asked to price them.

s03a.slug: SUNDAY · 8:35 AM · HOLY ROSARY — THE LINE
body: Hébert holds the host up over the paten in old fingers that don’t shake. “This is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. Happy are those who are called to his supper.”

“Lord, I am not worthy to receive you,” the church says, “but only say the word and I shall be healed,” and Tony behind him says it a word ahead of everybody, and the ushers come up the aisle to start the rows.

body.text: The pew empties into the aisle in its order: Mémère, then Jack, then Lena behind him, then Laney. Theo stands with the row and sits back down when it has gone past him, and a minute later Margot comes forward out of the pew behind to sit beside him, the two of them alone in the front pew of the Broussards. When Jack looks back from the aisle, Theo’s hands are on the back of the pew in front of him.

He was absolved on Friday at five past three in the morning, in the confessional two thousand miles behind him, and he goes up. The aisle is old tile, worn to a path down the middle. Mémère’s hat goes ahead of him at the pace of Mémère, behind an old man with a cane who holds his Saints cap over his heart up to the front. At the head of the side aisle Our Lady stands on her plinth with a rosary of real beads hung over her plaster hands. Behind him, at the edge of his eye, the hem of a black dress.
Three people ahead of him in the line, in her voice, exactly: *I want you to be able to.*
“The Body of Christ.”
“Amen.”

He holds out his hands, the left on the right, and Hébert lays the host in them. He takes it with his right hand, a step to the side, and crosses himself, and the quiet comes up through him the way heat comes up through the floor of Nonna’s kitchen in January, from somewhere under the house he has never been down to see.

When he turns up the side aisle Lena is at the front of the line with her chin up, receiving. Behind her Laney has her arms crossed over her chest, a Baptist braced for it, and Hébert puts his thumb to her forehead and blesses her, and calls her *chère*, and Laney comes away from it looking as though she has been handed something and has to decide where to put it. Somewhere behind Laney, Tony says his *Amen* to Hébert loud enough to close a deal.

He goes in past the aisle seat and kneels in his place. Mémère comes back at her own pace and lowers herself onto the end of the pew by the armrest, and gets her beads out. Up the side aisle Lena is coming back with her hands folded and her eyes down, past the Stations and the rack of red votive glasses, the medal out on top of the black dress where it has worked its way loose. She goes in past her grandmother’s knees and past his, and kneels beside him, and her shoulder is against his for the length of the communion hymn, which is one every grandmother in the building knows by heart, so the building sings it. Past her, at the end of the pew, Theo is studying his hymnal with tremendous concentration. It is open to Easter.

The pew empties into the aisle past him: Mémère from the end, then Lena and Laney stepping past his knees one after the other. He keeps his place, with Theo and Margot, while the rows go up, and kneels, and watches Tony and Celeste go by, and Kevin from the second pew, and the twins. He doesn’t go up.

Lena comes back up the side aisle with her hands folded and her eyes down and goes in past his knees again, and kneels beside him, and her shoulder is against his for the length of the communion hymn, which is one every grandmother in the building knows by heart, so the building sings it.

body: Kneeling after, with the hymn going on over his head, there is Mémère’s rosary clicking against the wood on one side, and Lena’s shoulder on the other, and in front of him the green and the gold and the candles, and a small old priest wiping out the chalice with a white cloth and taking his time about it. Under the hymn, barely, he can hear Lena: *Remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, that never was it known* — and then she goes too low for him.

choices.text: *Pray for Skye, by her name.*
choices.key: Kneeling after Communion at Holy Rosary you prayed for Skye.
response: *Mary Kate,* he says, inside, once.

He asks for the day on set to go right, and the wig to sit the way they want it, and the trailer to be warm. He asks that she sleep tonight, wherever they put her, and wake on her own. That’s the prayer. He doesn’t dress it up, and he says it from the first word to the last with Lena’s shoulder against his.
Up front Hébert sets the chalice down and goes to his chair and sits, and folds his hands on his stomach, and the church sits back with him, kneelers going up all down the nave, one after another.

choices.text: *Say Peter’s line, and mean it.*
choices.key: Kneeling after Communion at Holy Rosary you said Peter’s line and meant it. Depart from me, Lord.
response: The kneeler is wood under a skin of leather gone hard with use, and his knees ache on it, in the ordinary way.
*Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.*

He says it inside, to the end, and stays down. Nothing comes back. Lena’s shoulder doesn’t move from his. The hymn goes into its last verse. When the people around him sit back, Mémère sits last, pulling herself up by the pew in front, and she gives his sleeve a tug on her way down, as if he’s an altar boy who’s missed the bell.

choices.text: *Don’t ask for anything. Say thank you.*
choices.key: Kneeling after Communion at Holy Rosary you didn’t ask for anything. You said thank you.
response: *Thank you,* he says, inside, and then, because thank you wants an object: for the van, which got here. For the house, and the steps up to it. For the eggs. For Kevin’s driving sheet and Margot’s Gideon and Mémère’s chicory at a quarter to seven. For this pew, and the old wood, and the old woman on the end of it.
The next thing on the list has a face, and he stops there.

Up at the altar the boy with the cross yawns enormously behind his hand, and Hébert sits down in his chair, and the church sits back, and for a while there is only the organ finishing the hymn by itself.

s03b.slug: SUNDAY · 9:00 AM · HOLY ROSARY, THE STEPS
body: Hébert has his hand up for the last blessing and has got as far as *the Father* when somebody at the back, by the holy-water font, says it, not loud: *Who dat.* Somebody answers. By *the Son* it has gone down both side aisles, and Hébert raises his voice to get the Holy Spirit in over the top of it, and the church crosses itself in the middle of a chant, every hand, Mémère’s too. He puts his other hand up to stop it, a crossing guard at three o’clock, and gets nowhere, and he is laughing. “Go in peace to love and serve the Lord,” he says, and *Thanks be to God* comes back at him in the chant’s own time, and the chant goes out the open doors ahead of everybody and down the steps into Esplanade.
He is at the door when they get there, shaking hands. He takes Lena’s in both of his. “Magdalena,” he says. “You brought a delegation.”
Behind him in the line Mémère hands him over: “*Lucien. Le garçon de l’Ohio.*” Then Jack’s hand, and a good long look up at him from under white eyebrows. “So you’re the one from Ohio.”
“Yes, Father.”
“Hm.” Hébert gives the hand one more shake and lets it go. “Odile tells me you stayed in the house.”
He has already turned to Laney. “That was a beautiful service, Father,” Laney tells him, Dallas to the bone.
“Baptists welcome,” Hébert says. “Y’all bring the best casseroles.” And the line moves Jack out into the light.

body.text: At the bottom of the steps Kevin falls in beside him and puts a hand on his shoulder, and leaves it there a moment, and says nothing.
body.else: At the bottom of the steps Kevin falls in beside him, hands in his pockets, looking at the oaks. “Good to see you up there,” Kevin says.

body: Margot comes out behind them into the gray with her notebook already open against her forearm, and writes standing up. “Field note,” she says. “They were on their feet before he dismissed them.”

Across the street the oaks hold Esplanade over their heads like a roof somebody forgot to finish. Mémère is coming down the steps with Remy on one side of her and Theo on the other, Theo’s arm crooked for her at exactly the height cotillion teaches. And Lena is on the bottom step with her face turned up into the light, what there is of it, with her eyes shut.

journal.title: Fr. Lucien Hébert
journal.text: The pastor at Holy Rosary. He baptized all six of them, Lena says, and Lucille in January, in the third quarter. At the door he called her Magdalena, and Mémère handed me over to him: le garçon de l’Ohio. Sunday he preached on Peter in the boat: ask Him anyway; if He says no, the gumbo is still good. Mémère had already told him I stayed in the house.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the fundraiser: a room raised for a cause, handed to its opposition. Skye said she didn’t hand them the room, she introduced them to me, and she’s still voting for Boxer. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Four versions of Wednesday are going around Delgado, she says. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture. Monday night in the Fishbowl: six versions of Wednesday now. One has reached the Classics department. She wouldn’t read me any of them. Thursday night at the van she took the pie on her lap, for science, and told the van about men in some societies who may not speak to their mothers-in-law; everything goes through a third party. Radcliffe-Brown. Then she turned her recorder off. Friday it was eight versions of Wednesday. Then she drove Picacho to El Paso and wouldn’t stop for anything: there’s nowhere to stop, it’s the Chihuahuan Desert. Saturday at sunup she lent me a Gideon from the Santa Lucia Motor Court. Not God. A primary source. Sunday she attended the eight o’clock as an observer and was told to sit. She took her field notes on the church steps.

s04.slug: SUNDAY · 10:40 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH
body: Remy has a milk crate on the top step with a twin on either side of it, and he is packing it for the day: grocery sacks folded small, two pairs of work gloves, a roll of duct tape, and a stuffed alligator in a Saints helmet, unexplained. He has a black-and-gold tie knotted loose over a T-shirt. The block is already loud. Two houses down a man is standing on his porch rail to hang a flag, and a radio across the street is running the same pre-game half a second behind another one up the block.

“Carrollton’s rolling at eleven,” Remy says. “King Arthur at noon. Both an hour early, on account of the game.” He points the duct tape down the porch. “I got room for the twins, the redhead, the rich one and the professor.”
“I’m a sophomore,” Margot says.
“Professor.”
“I’d prefer *patron*,” says Theo, from the rail.
Laney already has her sunglasses on her head. “It’s *copper*, and I will fight you on a public street.”

“See, that’s a redhead talking.” Remy tapes the alligator’s helmet on tighter. Josie picks the lipstick tube up off the porch rail, caps it, and puts it in her pocket. Jude is already at the bottom of the steps by Remy’s car with his hands in his jacket.

Kevin is on the swing beside Mémère with a borrowed rosary across his knees. She claimed him for eleven o’clock somewhere between the church and the car, and he hasn’t argued. Now she puts her foot down on the boards and stops the swing.
“The gumbo tonight wants a roux,” she says. And then, with a turn of her head toward the house: “And Magdalena makes the roux.”

Lena is in the screen door. She’s out of her church clothes and into an old black T-shirt over a gray thermal, and she is pushing the thermal’s sleeves up her forearms, the left and then the right, past the elbow.
From somewhere down the hall, not loud, in a voice every Broussard on the porch hears anyway, Celeste says she needs hands for the trinity.
“Lose a twin, Remy,” Lena says, “and don’t come home.”
“Which twin?”
“Me,” says Josie. “Obviously.”

choices.text: Go Uptown with Remy.
Stay. Somebody has to cut the onions.

s04k.slug: SUNDAY · 11:00 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — THE ROUX
body: The kitchen smells of flour going brown in hot oil, raw onion, the andouille on Celeste’s board, and the chicory still keeping warm on the back burner from seven o’clock. The window over the sink is open a crack on the side yard. On the front burner sits a black iron pot that has been black since Eisenhower, with the flame under it turned down to a low blue fringe, and Lena stands at it with a wooden spoon worn flat along one side, down to a straight edge, by somebody dragging it across the bottom of that pot for longer than Lena has been alive.

Mémère has had a kitchen chair carried to the doorway and set down facing in, where she can see the stove and, by turning her head, straight down the hall to the foot of the attic stairs. Kevin is on a step stool in the hall behind her. Celeste is at the counter by the sink taking chicken thighs off the bone, three cuts to a thigh, quick and clean. Jack has the table: a cutting board, Celeste’s second-best knife, and a hill of yellow onions, green bells and celery that he is going to be at for some time. On the windowsill a boombox the size of a car battery has WWL on low, two men arguing about the Colts’ secondary as if one of them had money on it.

The rosary starts at eleven sharp. Mémère says the first half of every Hail Mary in French — *Je vous salue, Marie, pleine de grâce* — and Kevin answers with the second half from the hall in English, and at the stove Lena answers in French, just above a whisper, *Sainte Marie, Mère de Dieu*, without the spoon missing a turn. Jack answers in English, low, with the knife going. Between the third Glory Be and the next Our Father, Mémère leans forward on her chair and looks at his board.
“Smaller. *Plus petit.* You cut like a man from Ohio.”
“I am a man from Ohio, ma’am.”
“*Plus petit.*” And the Our Father, in French, from the top.

When the last decade is done and the Salve Regina after it, Kevin folds the beads into his shirt pocket and carries his stool off to the front room. Mémère crosses herself and points her own beads at the windowsill.
“Celeste. Those men talk like they’re paid by the word.”

Celeste rinses her hands, dries them, and turns the men off. Out of a shoebox on the sill she takes a cassette with GUMBO on the label in blue ballpoint, and puts it in, and pushes the button down with her thumb.

body.text: Tape hiss first, and then a fiddle, high and scratchy and in a hurry, and a man hollering in French over the top of it. He knows this one. He knows the steps. At the stove Lena’s spoon keeps its time around the pot.
body.else: Tape hiss first, and then a fiddle, high and scratchy and in a hurry, and a man hollering in French over the top of it. He knows this one. At the stove Lena’s spoon keeps its time around the pot.

body: In the doorway the toe of Mémère’s house shoe finds the time on the linoleum, one hard and two soft, and keeps it. Celeste, back at her board, says, “Bells next, baby. Then the celery.” He starts on the bells.
“What does your grandmother start with?” Lena asks, with the spoon going.
“Garlic in olive oil,” he says. “Low. If it goes brown she throws it out and starts over and doesn’t speak to you till Tuesday.”
“And then?”
“Then the tomatoes, and then five hours. Nonna goes to the seven o’clock. The pot goes to the ten with my mother.”
Lena laughs, high and surprised, into the steam, and the spoon jumps and goes on. Mémère wants to know what was funny, and Lena tells her in French, and Mémère hears it out and turns to Jack.
“Italian,” she says. “*Bon.* They cook.”

By the time the bells are done the roux has gone from the white of paste to something like a biscuit, and the smell has turned to toast. Lena reaches across Celeste’s board for a coin of andouille, and Celeste raps her knuckles with the back of the knife, and she eats it anyway. “Blond,” she says, chewing. “Now it starts being worth something. Now’s when people get bored and go answer the phone, and come back, and it’s black, and they cry, and they have to start over, and everybody at Thanksgiving knows.”
“What if the house is on fire?”
“You carry the pot out on the lawn and keep stirring,” she says. “And you pray for Remy.”

Mémère says something long in French, very pleased with it. There’s a word in the middle of it that sounds like *escalier*, and at the end her hands come up off her lap together and make the shape of a long gun.
“She says the stairs are steep,” Lena says.
Mémère looks straight at Jack. “I said, in my day, a boy carried a girl up those stairs, he married her or her daddy shot him.”
“*Mémère.*”
“Nobody’s shooting anybody before kickoff,” Celeste says, and goes on cutting.
Jack keeps cutting. The celery under his knife gets a good deal smaller than anybody asked for.

Halfway to done, Lena shakes out her right arm from the shoulder down and says, “Come here.” He wipes his hands on his jeans and comes. She puts the spoon in his hand and doesn’t let go of it. Her hand is over his, hot from the stove and dry with flour, and she takes him across the bottom of the pot and around the edge and across again, two strokes, three, so he gets the speed of it from her wrist instead of from being told.
“You never stop,” she says. “If you stop, it burns, and you start over.”

Then her hand is gone, and the spoon is his. He keeps it going. She stands at his shoulder and watches the pot. The heat comes up off the iron into both their faces, and a fleck of roux jumps the rim and lands on the back of his wrist and sticks there and goes on cooking.
“Cajun napalm,” Lena says. “Don’t touch your face.”

He doesn’t. He stirs. The flat edge of the spoon scrapes the iron on every pass, a dry sound under the wet one of the oil, and inside five minutes he understands about her arm. “Figure eights,” she says. “You’re leaving the edge. The edge is where it catches.” She reaches past him and turns the flame down a hair, and her forearm lies across his wrist while she does it, and then it doesn’t. At Nonna’s stove you get the elbow, where she can grab the spoon back off you. Lena has taken the shoulder. It is against the back of his arm, and every time the spoon comes round the near side of the pot it comes round toward her. She has put her hair up with a pencil through the knot, and the steam has got at the loose pieces by her ear. The fiddle goes on with its grievance. The roux goes from biscuit to peanut butter while he watches it, and the smell goes deep and nutty, like the bottom of a bag of something good, and she says “Peanut butter,” to confirm it, and stays at his shoulder.

Celeste comes past behind them with the cut-up chicken in a bowl on her hip, and on her way to the other burner she sets a hand flat between Jack’s shoulder blades, the way you’d steady a ladder, and takes it away again.

When it’s past peanut butter and still going darker, Lena leans in over the pot and looks. “Copper,” she says. “Laney’d be flattered.” She reaches over his hand and takes the spoon back. “Give it here. The end’s mine.” He gives it. She steps into the place he was standing, and he steps back to the table and his board, and she has the spoon going before his hand is off it.

She brings it the rest of the way herself. The spoon goes faster at the end, not slower, and she leans into it from the shoulder with her feet set wide on the linoleum and her lips moving on something, a count or a prayer, that he can’t make out from the table. Under her it goes darker than it ever went under him. The kitchen smells like pecans roasting. Celeste slides the bowl of chicken onto the counter at her elbow, and Mémère leans forward in the doorway with her hands folded on her beads to watch the color, and the tape gets to the end of one waltz and starts another one just like it.
Low, under the fiddle, with the spoon going round:
“I asked where you were. At Sully’s. Before the kickoff.”

choices.text: “I saw the picture. You on the table, with the bell.”
choices.key: Over the roux Lena said she’d asked where you were, at Sully’s, before the kickoff. You told her you saw the picture: her on the table with the bell.
response: “I saw the picture,” he says. “You on the table, with the bell.”
Her spoon stops.

“*Remue!*” says Mémère from the doorway, sharp as a slap on the hand, and Lena stirs. From then on Mémère doesn’t look at the pot any more. She looks at Jack, through the rest of the tape and the last of the roux, with her beads quiet in her lap.

“*Chocolat*,” she says at last. “Stop when it’s *chocolat*.” It is. Lena puts the spoon back in his hand — “Stir.” — and takes the board off the table and tips the trinity into the pot all at once. It goes in with a hiss like a rain squall on a tin roof, and a cloud comes up off the iron and fogs the window over the sink, and the side yard goes out of it, and the fiddle plays on the other side of the glass.

choices.text: “I was at a taco truck. I’m sorry I missed it.”
choices.key: Over the roux Lena said she’d asked where you were, at Sully’s, before the kickoff. You said you were at a taco truck, and you’re sorry you missed it.
response: “I was at a taco truck,” he says. “I’m sorry I missed it.”
“You should be,” she tells the roux. “Dale wept.” The spoon goes round twice. “He kept saying *forty-three years*. He’s from Michigan.”
“Theo said.”
“Theo cried too. Don’t let him tell you different.”

From the doorway Mémère watches the pot go dark, and says, when it’s time, “*Chocolat.* Stop when it’s *chocolat*.” Lena tips her head at his board without a word, and he brings it to the stove and scrapes the trinity in with the back of Celeste’s second-best knife. It goes in with a hiss and a cloud that comes up off the iron and fogs the window over the sink, and Lena stirs it under, and the kitchen smells of everything at once.

choices.text: “I know.”
choices.key: Over the roux Lena said she’d asked where you were, at Sully’s, before the kickoff. You said: I know. That was all.
response: “I know,” he says.
She nods at the pot.

The fiddle saws on. Jack finishes the last of the celery, small enough this time for anybody from Breaux Bridge, and Mémère watches the roux go darker, and says, when it’s right, “*Chocolat.* Stop when it’s *chocolat*.” Celeste is already there. She comes in at Lena’s elbow with Jack’s board on her forearm and tips the trinity in over both their hands, and it hits the iron with a hiss and a cloud that fogs the window over the sink, and the three of them stand in the steam of it, coughing, while Lena stirs.

s04p.slug: SUNDAY · 11:20 AM · ST. CHARLES AVENUE — CARROLLTON
s04p.music: Professor Longhair — “Go to the Mardi Gras”
body: The piano gets to them before the parade does. It comes out of two speakers somebody has propped on the sills of an upstairs window across the avenue, a left hand rolling downhill and a right hand tripping over it on purpose, and a man’s voice laid on top that would rather you heard it than understood it. They left Remy’s Suburban in a stranger’s driveway six blocks back, on Remy’s word that he knew the man, and now they come out of a side street onto the neutral ground, the long green strip down the middle of St. Charles Avenue, where the streetcar tracks run empty and are being stood on, and the ladders stand along the curb in rows with a kid’s seat bolted to the top of each and a kid strapped into it. A family under a pop-up tent has held the same twenty feet since six o’clock with a gas grill, an ice chest and a sign taped to the tent pole, MAMA’S SPOT.

The sky is thin and bright and just cold enough for coats, and everything under it is black and gold: jerseys, wigs, a baby in a bib, a man’s beard dyed to match. The parade is an hour early on account of the game, and the avenue is talking about the game anyway. The air smells of charcoal and spilled Abita and, underneath, the river. Manning’s name goes by on the wind about every fourth sentence, said like the name of a weather system. The last parade Jack stood at was Memorial Day on Market Street, the VFW and the Mooney band and two fire trucks, with applause as polite as a church’s. Nothing was thrown at anyone. Here a man on a porch rail across the way is already crying, with a beer in his hand, at nothing yet.

Remy plants the milk crate by a hydrant, and the first float comes down on them at the speed of a man walking a dog: a flatbed under crepe paper and plywood, three tiers high, with masked riders on every tier in satin and foil and, over the satin, Saints jerseys. The one on top is swaying with a plastic cup. He points a gold glove at nobody in particular and flings a double handful of beads at the crowd. “He’s gonna be on Bourbon by five,” Remy says, “and he don’t even know it yet.”

Laney is up on the crate before the beads land. She’s in a Saints jersey of Tess’s that comes to her knees, belted into a dress, with her sunglasses pushed up into her hair and both arms in the air. “Throw me something, *mister*!” It goes up the avenue in a Dallas soprano built to carry over a brass band and survive a key change, and the rider on the second tier turns his entire mask her way. The beads come down in a long rope and she takes them out of the air with one hand, and a pink cup with the other, and a stuffed football off her shoulder, and hops down and puts the armful into the lap of a girl on the nearest ladder. “Here, sugar. You’re going to want to hang on to those.” She is back on the crate with her arms up before the girl has finished saying thank you. “In Dallas,” she tells the avenue, “a parade is a Shriner on a tiny motorcycle and a judge waving. No one throws anything at you. I have been lied to my entire life.”
“Purple’s justice,” Remy tells Margot, who has asked. “Green’s faith. Gold’s power.”
“Rex assigned the meanings in the 1890s,” Margot says. “Before that they were colors.”
“Where do y’all keep her?” Remy asks Jack.
Josie has taken Margot in hand. “You can’t just stand there. They don’t throw to people standing there.”
“I’m attending as an observer.”
“Observers don’t get beads.”
“Observers get the footnote.”

“It’s not a gift if you don’t holler, it’s a delivery,” says Josie, and Margot folds her arms inside the long black coat and declines, on principle, and watches a marching band come around the bend in maroon wool and white plumes, sousaphones bobbing, the drum line stepping on every second beat. Beside Jack, Jude has stood at his left elbow all the way from the Suburban with his hands in his jacket pockets and said nothing, and he watches the band too. By the third float Jack has understood it as company.

On the next ladder over, a nine-year-old in a Brees jersey that comes to his shins is working the crowd from his seat on top. His mother stands under him with one hand on a rung. “Dominic, save your voice, baby, we got a *game*.” Dominic does not save his voice. He fills from the bottom up and lets go a THROW ME SOMETHING, MISTER you could land a plane by, and the rider on the nearest float swings around and fires a cup and a strand of beads that wraps his head twice.
Laney, down off her crate, pushes her sunglasses onto her nose to look at him. “That child has projection.”
“Gotta be Gentilly,” says Josie. “They start ’em early.”
“Tell him he’s in my throwing lane,” Laney says to Theo, with her eyes on the next float, and it takes Jack a second to find out she means him.
“He’s standing right here,” says Theo.
“I know exactly where he is.”

Jack takes a step to the left. Theo has been filming since the stranger’s driveway, in the camel coat, the iPhone held out at arm’s length, and on the fourth float Jack glances over at the screen and the screen is looking at him.
“That’s me.”
“Hm?” Theo doesn’t lower it.
“Your phone. That’s me.”
“Context,” says Theo.
“Context for what?”
“The floats.”
“The floats are behind me.”
“That’s what makes it context.” He keeps filming. A float goes by, and a dance troupe in gold sequins, and Theo says, easy, to the screen: “How was Mass?”
“I went up.”
“I know. I was in the pew.”
The drum line goes by with nothing on it. Then Theo swings the phone off Jack and onto the band, and holds it there, and studies the sousaphones with a concentration that would get him a scholarship.
“You’re filming a tuba.”
“Sousaphone. Different range.”

Behind them a rider on the next float is throwing medallion beads, plastic ones the size of a jar lid, and Josie, who has said all she has to, drops her arms and stops coaching. Margot takes her hands out of her coat. “Throw me something, mister,” she says. It is perfect. It is a low, carrying contralto with every consonant in place, and the rider turns round from three other people and hits her in the face with a medallion. Her glasses go crooked. The strand settles round her neck on its own.
“A gift economy,” Margot says, “in which the gift is thrown at your head. Mauss would have wept.”
“*Told* you,” says Josie.

A weight comes down over Jack’s head from the side, a long loop of purple beads, and settles on his collar. Laney is facing the avenue again with her arms back in the air. “Don’t make it a thing, fireman,” she tells the float, and goes back to hollering.
He lifts a loop off his collar and looks at it, and leaves it on.

Carrollton ends the way parades end, with a pickup and a man with a push broom, and the crowd doesn’t leave, because King Arthur is due at noon. Its riders are in gold capes and its floats are white and gold under crepe-paper turrets, and the medallion beads come down heavier than Carrollton’s, each with a crown stamped into the metal, so that when one lands on the pavement it rings. Laney catches six cups, two dozen strands and a gold plastic spear with a crown on the grip, and uses the spear to point out ladders. “You. You. *You.*” Cups arrive in their hands.

Across the avenue the piano has found its way back to the top and started over. A crown strand lands on Jude’s hood. He leaves his hands in his pockets and lets it hang there until a toddler on a man’s shoulders points, and then he lowers his head so the man can lift it off. He goes back to standing next to Jack.

By one the avenue has started to drift. A man scrapes his grill. A woman folds a chair and holds it against her chest, looks up the avenue at the next float and then at her husband, and then she’s walking. Half the neutral ground is going home to its televisions with the last float not yet by, a household at a time, shoulders up.
“They’re going to their seats,” Margot says, watching a family collapse a tent. “Whatever chair they had for the Vikings. Josie explained it over eggs. It’s a conservation strategy.”
“Don’t say it out loud,” says Remy, and knocks twice on the hydrant, and the man at the grill knocks on his grill.

“Last one,” Remy announces, to everyone. “Now or never.” The last float is a long time coming. On its top tier a rider in a gold cape is swinging a strand of the heavy beads around his head, searching the crowd for somebody to give it to. On the next ladder Dominic has found his second wind. And at the very back of the float another rider holds up something brown and round in both hands, like a trophy.
“Coconut,” says Remy.
“Zulu’s Mardi Gras morning, Remy,” Josie says.
“Somebody’s holding out.” Under the empty ladder next to them a man in an I WAS THERE FOR THE OVERTIME T-shirt is eating a boudin link, and looking from the coconut to Jack, and back.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard. Friday night at a gas station in El Paso, by the ice machine, he and Laney said it was a mistake. The whole thing. I agreed with them. He went in and paid for the gas himself. Sunday on St. Charles he filmed me instead of the floats and called it context. He asked how Mass was, and he already knew: he’d watched from the pew.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Monday night she and Theo were on the lounge floor with two legal pads side by side, and turned them over when I came in. A wedding seating chart, Theo said. Hypothetical. She took ink off my face with her thumb, and went cold again. Thursday night at the van she said she wasn’t Western Union and relayed everything anyway. She packed me a bag: FIREMAN, LARGE. Thirty hours. Behave. She told me Julian isn’t coming, like I’d care, and I told her so. Friday night in El Paso she broke a pill in half with her nail. It’s a prescription, Theodore. Saturday on Dupre Street Lena’s mother said So you’re my redhead, and Laney cried in her arms and didn’t say why. Sunday at Carrollton she put a strand of purple beads on me without looking. Don’t make it a thing, fireman. She gave everything else she caught to kids on ladders.

choices.text: Save the best throw you catch for Lena.
choices.key: At Carrollton and King Arthur you caught a medallion bead with a crown on it and saved it for Lena.
response: The rider on the top tier has been looking for somebody the length of the block, and he finds him: a gold glove comes out of the cape, points at the man in the purple beads, and lets go. The strand turns over once in the air, a flash of gold, and Jack’s hand is up and it’s in it. It is heavier than anything else he has caught today, with a crown stamped in the medallion, and he knows where it is going. It goes into the inside pocket of the Carhartt, and he keeps his hand over the outside of the coat through the crush that follows.
Theo sees him do it, and swings the 3GS onto a passing float. Laney, three feet away, says nothing at a volume that carries to the river.

Remy puts a plastic whistle between his teeth and blows until the twins and the redhead and the rich one and the professor and the Ohio boy are all facing him, and then walks backward toward the side street with the milk crate held over his head like a standard, and they follow it.

choices.text: Get into a hollering contest with a nine-year-old.
choices.key: At Carrollton you lost a hollering contest to a nine-year-old. He gave you a cup out of pity.
response: “HEY!” Jack tries, in the voice that has called Rosie in off Glenwood Avenue since she could walk. “UP HERE! HEY!” The flat Youngstown vowels go out over the neutral ground and a pigeon leaves a streetlight.

On the next ladder Dominic fills up until the jersey lifts off his stomach, and lets go. THROW ME SOMETHING, MISTER. The rider on the top tier of the float swings round like he’s been shot at and throws the boy all of it. Margot, who was not asked, rules from the curb that in the literature the elder is expected to lose. Dominic looks down at Jack, kind to the bone, and holds out a pink cup. “You can have this. It’s okay.” He thinks about it. “You’ll get better.”

Remy counts heads at the curb with a finger for each, reaches seven on the second try, and starts them toward the side street with the milk crate on his shoulder, saying the number to himself the length of the block.

choices.text: Climb a stranger’s ladder for the coconut.
choices.key: At Carrollton you climbed a stranger’s ladder for a coconut. It was a stuffed football. Remy called you brother-in-law in front of the whole neutral ground.
response: “Go ahead, young man,” says the man in the overtime shirt, who sets down his boudin and takes hold of the ladder’s legs with both hands. It is made for a seven-year-old’s weight in a seat the size of a mixing bowl. Jack goes up past the third rung to the one under the little seat, one hand on the seat and one in the air, with the neutral ground swaying slightly under him and the rider at the back of the float looking down.

The rider winds up sidearm. The brown thing comes at his chest in a soft arc and he gets both arms round it. It is a stuffed football. There is a fleur-de-lis embroidered on it. It is nothing like a coconut.

The man at the ladder’s foot applauds, hands up high over his head so the neutral ground can see. “Brother-in-law!” Remy yells, at a volume that turns heads on both sides of the avenue, and goes on yelling it. Josie takes one look at him, and takes him by the sleeve and Jude by the hood, and starts for the side street, and the rest of them fall in behind the only one with a plan.

s05.slug: SUNDAY · 4:20 PM · DUPRE STREET — THE HOUSE THAT CAN’T SIT DOWN
body: By twenty past four the sun has got down into the oaks at the end of Dupre Street, and it comes in the front windows low and yellow and lies across the rug, the couch, and the big television, where Channel 4 has had the pre-game on since two. On the screen it is still bright afternoon in Miami. Seventy-some thousand people are finding their seats in the sun. In the house on Dupre Street the couch is empty and the room is full.

body.text: Remy gets them home four hours after King Arthur, by way of a short cut through Uptown that he still believes in and a cousin’s porch on Napoleon Avenue where he stopped for a plate of boudin. He comes up the steps first with the twins and a pillowcase of throws over his shoulder, and Jack comes up behind him with Laney’s purple beads still round his neck. It went on without him: Lena’s roux in Mémère’s big pot on the back burner, the lid cocked, and Mémère’s spoon laid across it.
body.else: Jack has been in this house since the roux. The gumbo on the back burner is the one he cut the onions for, five hours on, down to dark in Mémère’s big pot with the lid cocked, and he has been sent from it twice since, once for andouille and once to the attic for the folding chairs. The parade came home at one with Remy and a pillowcase of throws. Laney fell asleep sitting up on the porch swing with a stuffed football in her lap, and Theo spent an hour explaining the Colts’ secondary to Tony, who let him.

body: For an hour now the house has been filling. People come up the steep steps without knocking and in through the screen door with their hands full: the lady from across the street with a king cake in a bakery box, purple and green and gold sugar coming off it onto the cellophane; a couple from the corner with a foil pan of jambalaya; and a big slow man in a Saints visor from two doors down who brings his own cooler of Abita, his own folding chair, and a boombox, which he sets on the porch rail and turns up. People stand in the front room with a bowl in one hand and a spoon in the other and their eyes on Miami, and when one of them shifts to let somebody by, everybody shifts, a slow tide of elbows going round the furniture.

On the porch rail the boombox is all piano and horns and a voice going up and up about Carnival when a man comes up the steps. Jack knows him for a Broussard from the bottom step: Tony’s face with less of it, shorter and quicker and brown as a saddle, in a gold Saints windbreaker, with a folding chair under one arm and a leash in the other hand. At the end of the leash, taking the steps one at a time and stopping on each to reconsider, is a basset hound in a black-and-gold bandana.
“*Nonc Clovis!*” Josie yells, and the twins come out from under the dining table at a run.

At the top of the steps Clovis finds the tune and comes in with the boombox, loud, every word of the first verse right, conducting the porch with the leash hand. At the end of the verse he stops singing as if somebody had pulled his plug, and the song goes on into the chorus without him, and he lets it, and comes in.

“That’s Nonc Clovis. Daddy’s baby brother,” Remy says, going past Jack with a beer. “He knows the first verse of everything. Only the first. Him and Daddy and them put this house back after the water, and Nonc sang the first verse of every song on the radio for two years straight. Mama about killed him.”
Clovis sets up his chair inside the door and looks Jack over. “This the Ohio boy?”
“Yes, sir.”

“Browns.” Clovis shakes his head over it. He holds out the leash, and Jack, not knowing what else to do with it, takes it. “That’s Aints III. I named the first one in 1980. Bag year.” He sits. The dog sits on Jack’s foot. “The first one was ashamed. This one’s made his peace.”
Lena comes through from the kitchen with a stack of Mémère’s heavy bowls against her hip and her free arm going round her uncle’s neck on the way past.

body.text: “He cut the onions,” she tells Clovis, over the bowls. Clovis looks at Jack, and through the kitchen door at the pot, and back. “Small?” “Small enough,” Lena says. “Mémère only had to tell him twice.”

He has had it in his inside pocket all afternoon, with his hand over it most of the way home. He takes it out now and holds it out to her: the medallion bead, a gold crown stamped on the disk. Lena looks at it. She puts the bowls down on the arm of the couch and takes it from him and puts it over her head, and it comes down on top of the Miraculous Medal, the crown over the Virgin, and she picks up the bowls again and carries them on into the kitchen without a word.

body: In the kitchen Celeste puts an empty Igloo into his arms on her way past the stove. “Ice, baby,” she whispers. “The freezer in the shed.” He gives the leash to Josie and goes down the back steps with it, and comes back up them with it full and heavy against his chest. Celeste points him up the hall with her knife: the porch, for the man in the visor.

Luc is at the counter when he comes in with it. He is in uniform, the dark blue shirt with the patch and the badge, the belt with everything on it, a radio on his shoulder muttering numbers to itself, and he is eating a bowl of gumbo standing up, fast and neat, with his back to the window. “All hands in the Quarter tonight,” Tony says, coming through with a dish towel. “Every badge in the city.” Luc doesn’t add to it. He rinses his bowl and puts it in the drainer, and kisses his mother on the side of the head at the stove, and comes up the hall behind Jack and the ice. In the front room he bends down in front of Mémère’s armchair, a long way down, and she puts her thumb on his forehead and makes a small cross there, and says something in French for him only.
On his way out he stops in front of Jack, who is stuck in the crush by the door with the cooler in his arms. Luc looks at him. It isn’t long.
“Take care of the house.”

And he is out the screen door and down the steps. The room goes on eating. When Jack turns around, Lena is at the far end of the hall in the kitchen doorway with the ladle held up out of the pot, and a drop of gumbo is running down the handle onto the inside of her wrist. Her eyes go from the screen door to him. She puts her wrist to her mouth and turns back to the stove.
Remy climbs up on the coffee table and says, “*Seats.*”

body.title: Masking tape along the bottom of the television, in purple marker
body.text:
VIKINGS SEATS. DO NOT MOVE.
MAMA — COUCH (CORNER) · REMY — ARM · TESS + LUCILLE — FLOOR BY TV · BEAU — WHEREVER TESS SAYS · NONC — HIS CHAIR BY THE DOOR · MÉMÈRE — HER CHAIR · JOSIE + JUDE — UNDER THE TABLE · DADDY — PORCH · LUC — WORKING
NO NEW SEATS. NO TRADES.

body: “I wrote it down,” Josie says from under the dining table, “so there’s no arguing.”

Since the NFC Championship, Tess explains from the floor by the television, with Lucille asleep on her chest in the black-and-gold cap, every Broussard watches from wherever they sat when Hartley’s kick went through, and they have not lost since. Theo gets up off the arm of the couch without being told. Celeste takes her corner, Remy his arm. Clovis and the twins and Mémère are already where the tape says.
Margot reads the tape. “So the seating chart is load-bearing.”
“Everything in this house is load-bearing,” Remy says. “Daddy built it.”
“*Me*, I built the stairs,” says Clovis.

Tony comes up the hall with a kitchen chair hooked over his forearm and his radio in the other hand, a battered silver transistor with a coat hanger for an antenna. He stops in front of the television long enough for Miami to go by on his face.
“I was on the porch for the overtime,” he tells the room. “I’m on the porch.”

He goes out. Through the screen Jack watches him lean over the boombox on the rail. “Sorry, Ferd. I need the rail.” He unplugs it in the middle of the chorus, and the transistor goes up in its place, and the WWL men come on, low and fast and serious, and Ferd moves his folding chair over beside Tony’s kitchen chair, and the two of them sit with their backs to the window and listen to a pre-game they could watch by turning their heads.

Mémère takes the guests in hand. She puts her slipper to the footstool and slides it across the rug to Margot — “You.” — and Margot sits on it with her knees up under her chin. A dining chair has appeared at Mémère’s elbow, and Mémère pats it, and Kevin, her rosary partner since eleven, sits down in it and takes back the beads she hands him. Celeste whispers Theo and Laney down to the far end of the couch, and they go, and sit very close together and very straight and take a deep interest in the coin-toss graphics.
Which leaves Jack, and Lena, come out of the kitchen with a bowl of gumbo in each hand. There is no seat in this house for either of them.
“We weren’t here for the Vikings,” Lena tells her grandmother.
Mémère looks at them over her beads.
“Those two,” she says. “On the floor. In front. Where I can see them.”
Lena hands him one of the bowls. She sits down cross-legged on the rug in front of the couch, with her back against it below her mother’s knees, and settles her bowl in her lap.
“She means it as a punishment,” she says.

She doesn’t move over. She has sat down in the middle of the rug, and the middle is where he sits. His knee is against hers. Her shoulder is against his arm. Aints III comes round the coffee table and lies down across both their feet with a groan from somewhere deep in the bandana. The gumbo is dark and smoky and hotter than it looks, and the heat of it comes up slow, after you’ve decided it isn’t coming. A piece of her hair has come loose and lies along the side of her neck, down to the collar of her shirt, where the chain of the medal goes under it. He eats his gumbo.

He has had three spoonfuls when the RAZR goes off against his hip. On the outside screen, a long 330 number he has never saved and would know in his sleep. He hands Lena his bowl and gets up off the floor, and Lena’s eyes come up off Miami and go with him as far as the kitchen door.

He opens it. The same flat woman. “This is a prepaid call from —” and into the gap, fast, his brother’s own voice: “Danny.” “— an inmate at Trumbull Correctional Institution. This call is subject to monitoring and recording. To accept, press one.”
He presses one.
“Professor.”
“Dan.”

Behind Danny, the dayroom: a television up high and loud, the same pre-game, half a second ahead of the one in the front room, and a room of men talking over it. “Gina says you’re at the Saints girl’s house for the Super Bowl and you’re calling it a road trip.”
“I didn’t call it anything.”
“That’s what I mean.”

Jack sits down on the back steps. The yard is in shadow already, the big boil pot washed out and turned upside down on the picnic table, and over the roof of the shed the sky is going the clear deep blue it goes before it gives up.
“Where are you right now?” Danny says.
“Back steps. Her old man’s out front on the porch with a radio. He won’t watch.”
“He won’t watch the *Super Bowl*.”
“He couldn’t watch the overtime against the Vikings. He went out on the porch with the radio, and they won. So now he’s on the porch.”
Danny laughs, low. “That’s a smart man. That man knows how it works.” The dayroom yells at something. “Who you got?”
“Who do you think.”
“Me too. The room’s got Indianapolis except me and Reggie, and Reggie’s got whoever I got.” Somebody behind him wants the volume up and gets it. “Ma lit a candle for the kicker again.”
