“Hartley.”
“She don’t know his name. She lit it for *the kicker*. Side altar at St. Brigid’s, a dollar in the box. Gina says Father Dom watched her do it and pretended he didn’t see.”

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first. Thursday at seven in the morning she called me herself, from Dupre Street, on a number the redhead gave her. She knew I’d said yes. She called anyway: I don’t come because the rich boy asked me, I come because she asked me. Don’t bring nothing. Come to this house first — I said it back to her. Lena told her not to call. Saturday night on the porch she cancelled Theo’s hotel. You sleep here. Boys in the attic. She sleeps in the front room, where she can see the stairs. Sunday she was dressed for the eight o’clock before seven, in her chair with the lamp on. Two of you are up; the other sleeps like a Protestant. For the game she put Lena and me on the floor, in front, where she could see us.

journal.title: Clovis Broussard
journal.text: Nonc Clovis. Tony’s baby brother, Remy says; one of the brothers who put the house back. Built the stairs, he says. Knows the first verse of everything, and only the first. His dog is Aints III, in a Saints bandana; he named the first one in 1980, the bag year.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas, his twenty-third, he called from Trumbull and got Skye. Gina’s envelope hadn’t come — two cards in it, she says, and one with a candle. Skye’s letter came, in capitals. Ma wouldn’t tell him the name of the song. Skye told him how I tricked her — a long caper, a love spell in Gloria’s crust — and he laughed till they told him to keep it down. Family news, he said. Then she told him what really happened in Montecito, and he coughed for a while. She asked him to call again. I told him she’s the one I can tell the truth to. He said I’m not subtle. He’s still going with the trick. Super Bowl Sunday he called from the dayroom before the kickoff. Gina told him I’m at the Saints girl’s house and calling it a road trip. Ma lit a candle for the kicker again; she doesn’t know his name. The dayroom has Indianapolis, except Danny and Reggie.

choices.text: “I wish you were here for this.”
response: “Me too,” Danny says. “I’d be out on the porch with the old man. I like him already.” Somebody near the phone wants to know is he gonna be all day. “Watch the game, Professor. All of it.”

The woman cuts in. “You have one minute remaining.” They spend it on nothing much: the dayroom chili, the cold in Leavittsburg, and Reggie’s opinion of Peyton Manning, which Danny declines to repeat on a recorded line.
When Jack comes back in and sits down on the rug, his bowl is waiting on the floor in his place with the spoon standing up in it. Lena looks at him once, and back at Miami, and doesn’t ask.

choices.text: “Tell Ma the kicker says thanks.”
response: “I’ll tell her. She’ll light another one.” Danny’s voice has a grin in it. “She’s gonna have that side altar lit up like Christmas by the fourth quarter. Father Dom’s gonna have to call the fire department.”
“You have one minute remaining,” says the woman.
“Watch the game, Professor,” Danny says. “All of it.”

Back in the front room Aints III has taken his half of the rug and is asleep on it. Lena puts her hand on the dog’s backside and shoves, and the dog gets up and lies down again on the far side of her, sighing, and Jack sits where it was, warm.

choices.text: “It’s complicated, Dan.”
response: “It’s complicated, Dan.”
A silence on the line the length of a dayroom.
“Okay,” Danny says.
“You have one minute remaining.”
“Watch the game, Professor. All of it.”

The line clicks, and it’s the yard again. When he goes back in, Lena hands him his bowl, still warm; she has had it on her own knee. Somewhere toward Esplanade a car horn is blowing the Who Dat over and over.

s06.slug: SUNDAY · 5:25 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH — THE PHONE THAT RINGS AT THE KICKOFF
body: The anthem comes through the screen door with the volume up full, Carrie Underwood alone at a microphone over seventy thousand people in Miami, and the front room gets to its feet for it. Celeste stands at her corner of the couch with a hand on Remy’s shoulder. Mémère comes up out of her armchair on Kevin’s arm and stands with the beads hanging from the hand she holds over her heart. Clovis has his visor off and pressed to his chest. The twins have come out from under the table. At the far end of the couch Laney has her chin up and is mouthing every word, and Margot stands because everybody else is standing, hands in her back pockets, watching them do it. Lena stands on the rug beside him in her socks with her hands clasped behind her back. Lucille sleeps through it on her mother’s shoulder in the black-and-gold cap.

It ends, and the house yells, and the yell comes back down Dupre Street out of every open door on the block, a hair ahead or a hair behind, depending on whose set it is. The coin goes up in Miami. The room takes the coin personally.

When the teams go out to line up, Jack gets up off the rug with the RAZR in his hand. She asked him for a call at the kickoff. The screen door bangs behind him on its spring, and through the screen he sees Lena’s eyes come off Miami to the door.

Out here it’s going on dusk. The sun is down behind the houses across the street and the sky over them is going, and the porch light isn’t on yet, so the light comes from the windows: every house on Dupre Street with its door open and its television going, the same blue flicker on a row of porch ceilings down to the corner. The street itself is empty. Cars parked solid on both sides, fleur-de-lis on the bumpers, and not a soul on the sidewalk, not a bicycle, not a dog. A city has gone indoors at once and is holding still in there.

Ferd’s folding chair stands empty by the rail with an Abita sweating on the boards beside it; he went in for the anthem and hasn’t come back. Tony hasn’t moved. He sits in the kitchen chair with his back to the window and his elbows on his knees, and the transistor stands on the rail at his elbow with its face turned toward him and the coat-hanger antenna pointed east, at Miami, in case that helps. The WWL men are on it, fast and low and already hoarse. Tony’s eyes are shut. His lips are going. He doesn’t look round when the door bangs, or when Jack sits down on the top step a yard from his shoe.
Jack opens the RAZR to call her, and it rings in his hand, open, with his thumb still on its way to the keys: SKYE (MISFIT), across the inside screen. She got there first. He presses the green key.
“Don’t say hello,” Skye says. “Is it on? Tell me it isn’t on yet.”
“They’re lining up.”

“Good. I made it.” On her end something hums, a space heater or a generator, and under the hum, small and tinny, a television that isn’t his: the same game, the same men in the same booth, half a second behind the radio at Tony’s elbow. “I’m in the trailer. It’s three-thirty here. It’s *Sunday*. Nobody on this crew knows it’s Sunday. I told the makeup lady at lunch, and she said, ‘Is it?’ and went back to her crossword.”
“How’s Canada?”
“Damp. Polite. The geese are still the size of Labradors.”
“What are you watching it on?”

“Kyle’s laptop. Kyle is a PA. Kyle is from Fort Wayne, Indiana, and he is the only person in this province who cares, and he cares for the wrong team, and he has lent me his laptop and his hat. I’m in a Colts cap, Jack.”
“You said into a wig.”

“I’m wearing it into the wig. Cassie’s wig. It’s a long story.” A chair creaks under her, a chair that has been sat back in before. “It’s auburn, it took an hour, and it’s held onto my actual head with about forty pins, so it can’t come off between setups, so the cap goes on top. I look like a Colts fan who’s been through something.”
“You said quietly.”

“I am cheering quietly. Kyle and I have a chant. It’s very quiet. It’s mostly eyebrows.” The heater hums. “There are three other people in here and none of them care. The makeup lady has her crossword. A driver named Gord is asleep sitting up with a bran muffin in his hand. And Cassie’s stand-in, who is wearing the wig’s little sister, asked me which ones are the Saints, and I said the ones in the gold pants, and she said, ‘Oh, nice,’ like it was something they’d decided this morning.”
Jack laughs, and keeps it down for the porch.
“Where are you?” Skye says. “Don’t say a porch.”
“A porch.”
“Who’s on it?”
“Mr. Broussard.”
“Do him,” she says. “Three sentences.”
Tony is a yard from his shoulder with his eyes shut. Jack bends his head down toward the steps and keeps his voice under the radio.

“He sells fish on Banks Street, and in 1980 he wore a bag over his head at the Dome, and he’s been sending God the bill for it ever since. He couldn’t watch the Vikings, so he’s out here with his eyes shut and a radio with a coat hanger in it. His lips are going, and it isn’t the rosary.”
“Oh, I love him,” Skye says. “Tell him I’m sorry about the Colts in advance. Tell him I’m *personally* sorry.”
Jack looks at Tony. Tony’s lips go on moving.
“He’s on the other line.”
“Then I’ll hold.” Paper moves on her end, a page, a cover. “I have news. I bought it.”
“Bought what?”

“*The Moviegoer*. At the airport in San Francisco on Friday, at the newsstand, between a book about abs and a book about a vampire. Because of the margins. I read it on the plane, and the plane wasn’t long enough, so I finished it in the back of the car with the fleece man, and he asked me if it was any good, and I said I didn’t know yet. It hadn’t been read to me.”
“And?”

“And I have a note. For Binx.” A page turns on her end, and turns back. “Binx goes to the movies so his street will be real. I’ve *been* the movie since I was eleven. Being in it doesn’t make anything real either. You know what does? A man reading you something rude at a gas pump.”

Down the block a screen door opens and a man yells into the street for somebody named Darnell to get in here, it’s starting, and the door slaps shut again. Jack sits with the phone against his ear and his other hand over his mouth.
“Yeah,” he says.

“Okay,” Skye says. “Enough literature.” And then the voice comes down, close to the phone, low, the one she keeps for him, in a trailer in Canada with a crossword going on three feet away. “Wardrobe let me have your shirt back for lunch. Ten minutes. Cassie’s very possessive; it had to be negotiated.” The chair creaks. “I’m not telling you what else I had on.”
Jack looks for some time at a Buick parked across the street.
Tony’s eyes stay shut.
“I owe you a picture,” Skye says.
“Do you.”
“Not today. The wardrobe lady sits right outside that door, and she has opinions about my elbows.” And then, in the same breath, the same size: “Did you go up this morning?”
“I went up.”

“Good.” She says it short, and then she yawns, enormously, into the phone. “I’m so tired, Jack. I’ve been Cassie since six. Cassie cried in the rain at eleven and again at two, and the rain is a man named Russ on a ladder with a hose, and I have to go cry in front of Russ again in about five minutes.” The little television behind her goes to a commercial, a Canadian bank, a man in a canoe. “Hang on.”
A click, and the television in Burnaby is gone. There’s only the heater, and her breathing, close.
“There,” she says. “I turned Canada off. I wanted to hear the kickoff where you are.”
Jack takes the phone down from his ear and holds it out in the air between the radio and the screen door, and Tony keeps his eyes shut.

In Miami the ball goes up. It comes over the transistor and through the screen door at the same time, the WWL man’s voice climbing with it and the house going up underneath, a yell and a groan and Mémère saying something sharp in French and Remy saying something worse in English, and a half-second after that Dupre Street does it again out of every open door on the block, and down at the corner somebody leans on a car horn in the rhythm of the Who Dat. Tony’s hands close into fists.
Jack puts the phone back to his ear. Skye is laughing.

“Oh, I *heard* that,” she says. “I heard the *street*.” Two knuckles knock on a door on her end, and a man’s voice through it says they’re ready for her in the rain. “That’s Russ,” Skye says. “That’s my hose.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south. Friday at a truck stop under Picacho Peak she called from Burnaby. Wardrobe took my flannel: Cassie wears it; it got the part. The geese are the size of Labradors. I read her one of Hale’s rude ones at the pump. Saturday night she called again after wrap, and I read her two more, on the Broussards’ front steps. I told Lena’s little sister who she is. My girlfriend. In Canada. She wants a call at the kickoff. Sunday at the kickoff I had the phone open to call her, and it rang in my hand. She was in a trailer in Burnaby in a Colts cap, wearing it into Cassie’s wig. She bought her own *Moviegoer* at the airport and read it on the plane. Being in the movie doesn’t make anything real either, she says. She owes me a picture. She turned her TV off to hear the kickoff on Dupre Street.

choices.text: “Love you. Go cheer for the wrong people.”
choices.key: At the kickoff Skye called first, from a trailer in Burnaby, in a Colts cap. On Tony’s porch you told her you love her.
response: “Love you,” he says. “Go cheer for the wrong people.”
He doesn’t bring it down for the porch. It goes out over the rail into Dupre Street at the size he says everything else, with Tony a yard away.
“Love you,” Skye says. “Go be loud.” The knuckles again, and Russ. “Bye, Who Dat.”

The RAZR shuts on its cracked hinge. Tony’s eyes stay shut. He reaches out to the rail and takes the transistor by its two top corners and turns it a little further toward himself, until its face is square on his, and sets his elbows back on his knees.
Jack gets up off the step. As the screen door opens under his hand, behind him Tony says to the radio, “*Huh.*”
The WWL men go on talking to him about field position.

choices.text: “Tell the wig the Colts are favored by five.”
choices.key: At the kickoff Skye called first, from a trailer in Burnaby, in a Colts cap. You told her to tell the wig the Colts are favored by five.
response: “Tell the wig the Colts are favored by five.”
“The wig knows,” Skye says. “The wig has money on it. Kyle set the line.” The knuckles again, harder; Russ is not a patient hose. “Bye, Who Dat.”

He folds the phone shut. Tony hasn’t moved; his lips haven’t stopped. Jack gets up off the top step and pulls the screen door open, and the spring stretches and sings and brings the door round after him, and it catches him on the heel on his way in.

choices.text: “You’d like this porch. You’d have him doing his voice in ten minutes.”
choices.key: At the kickoff Skye called first, from a trailer in Burnaby, in a Colts cap. You told her she’d like this porch. Five minutes, she said.
response: “You’d like this porch,” he says. “You’d have him doing his voice in ten minutes.”
“Five,” Skye says. “I’d have the bag story by the second quarter, and I’d have the bag.” Russ knocks again. She doesn’t hurry for him. “Bye, Who Dat.”
The hinge creaks shut. He sits a moment longer on the step with it in his hand, and Tony goes on with God, and Jack gets up and lets himself into the noise.

s06a.slug: SUNDAY · 6:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT ROOM — THE FIRST QUARTER
body: The window behind Mémère’s lamp has gone dark blue, and the only other light in the front room comes off Miami.

The Saints get the ball first and give it back. The Colts take it down the field in a straight line, Manning at the line with his hands going, pointing at things and changing them, and when it stalls Stover kicks it through from thirty-eight and it’s three to nothing. The Saints get the ball and give it back again. The Colts go the length of the field a second time, slower and worse, and Manning finds Garçon in the end zone, and it is ten to nothing, and the front room of a raised shotgun on Dupre Street takes it every way a room can.

Clovis gets up out of his folding chair by the door and sings the first verse of “When the Saints” straight at the television, a cappella, loud enough to rattle the screen, and at the end of the first verse he stops, as advertised, and sits back down, and the second verse goes unsung. Mémère’s beads go faster. Kevin, on the dining chair at her elbow, keeps up with her a decade behind and losing ground. Remy has slid down the arm of the couch until he is mostly on Celeste, with his Saints cap over his face.
“It’s early,” Celeste whispers, to Remy, to the room, to the cap.
“Mama says it’s *early*,” Josie relays from under the dining table, and Jude, beside her, eats a Zapp’s.

On the floor by the television Tess has Lucille up on her shoulder, and Lucille is asleep through all of it with her fists up by her ears, like a very small fighter between rounds. Aints III gets up off Jack’s feet, turns around twice, and lies back down facing away from the screen.
“This is structure,” Theo announces from the far end of the couch. “Every great sports picture is down ten in the first act. You don’t make a movie about the team that’s up ten.”
“Theo,” Laney says, with her fingers sunk in a stuffed football from Carrollton, “I will put you on that porch.”
Margot, on the footstool, with her knees up under her chin: “Fascinating. The room has gone directly from denial to bargaining. It skipped anger.”
“It did not skip anger,” says Remy, under the cap.
The camera finds number 93 on the Colts’ sideline, bouncing on his toes between series, and Lena, beside Jack on the rug, says through her teeth, “Look at him. Indianapolis lies about ankles.”

At the break the room breathes out and half of it goes for the kitchen. Remy lifts the cap. On the big screen the cars and the beer give way to something quieter: a woman with her hair done nicely, talking soft into the camera about the son she nearly lost, and the son, when he comes, is Tim Tebow, coming in from the side of the frame to take his mother down in a tackle, which is the joke, and then a web address, and then it’s a car again. Thirty seconds.
“*Gator*,” Remy says, with feeling, and puts the cap back over his face.

Margot has not moved. “I’d like to be very precise about this,” she says. “For years CBS hasn’t taken advocacy in the Super Bowl. They turned down MoveOn in 2004. This year they took that one. And this same week they turned down an ad for a dating site, because it was two men on a couch, kissing.” She lets her chin come off her knees. “So the policy is: advocacy is fine if it’s *your* advocacy.”
She looks at Kevin. Kevin is looking at the television. His hands are on his knees.
“It’s a mother saying she’s glad she had her kid,” Jack says. “If that’s too controversial for television, television’s got a problem.”

“It’s a mother saying it in thirty seconds bought by an organization with a legislative agenda,” Margot says, “on the network that just told two men their couch wasn’t fit for Sunday. Which is advocacy, Jack, which you know, and which you’re delighted about.”
“I am delighted about it.”
“I know. It’s unbearable.”

Lena has been eating Zapp’s out of the bag in her lap one at a time, and she points the next one at the screen, where the car is now going up a mountain. “Y’all are both wrong. Two and a half million dollars. Do you know how many diapers two and a half million dollars is? In this city? Charity’s been shut since the water. There are girls in this city riding two buses with a baby on their hip to see a doctor in a trailer, girls who don’t have a Heisman coming, and somebody had two and a half million dollars and spent it on *thirty seconds*.”
“That’s not the —”

“It is *exactly* the.” She eats the chip. “And it wasn’t brave. It was careful. Thirty seconds and nothing in it a network lawyer could get a splinter off. It’s a holy card. It’s a very nice holy card. You could hand it out at a wake.”
“Careful’s how you get it on CBS.”
“Careful’s how you get it on CBS and nowhere else.”
Her knee is against his on the rug through all of it, and takes no part in the argument.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, from the dining chair, “it’s the first quarter.”
Through the screen door, from the porch, at the volume of a man who sells fish for a living: “*Y’ALL HUSH.*”
The room hushes. In the quiet the transistor on the rail can be heard going on outside about third down, and Mémère’s beads, and the refrigerator.
At the far end of the couch Laney has the stuffed football turned over in her hands. She is still looking at the screen where the mother was, though it’s a truck now.
“It was just his mama,” she says.

choices.text: *Take Margot on, one more round.*
response: “A dating site isn’t a cause,” Jack says. “It’s a dating site. CBS turns down commerce every year.”
“They’re running GoDaddy tonight,” Margot says at once. “A web host, selling cleavage. Commerce is fine. Cleavage is fine. It wasn’t the commerce they said no to, Jack. It was the couch.”

“Then they’re hypocrites,” Jack says. “Fine. Make them take both or neither, and I’ll live with neither. That’s a fight with CBS. It doesn’t make the mother wrong. You’re grading the network. I’m grading her.”
Margot regards him from the footstool. “You concede the network and keep the mother.”
“I keep the mother.”
“That’s the first decent argument anyone in this state has given me since Saturday,” she says. “I’m experiencing pleasure. It’s probably the gumbo.”

choices.text: “Lena’s right about the diapers.”
response: “Lena’s right about the diapers,” Jack says.
Lena turns her head and looks at him, close, with a Zapp’s stopped halfway to her mouth.
“Write that down, Margot,” she says.
“I don’t take dictation.”

Lena eats the chip and turns back to the screen with the corner of her mouth still up. Under the dining table Josie tells Jude the first quarter doesn’t count, and Jude, who has not said a word to Jack all weekend, nods.

choices.text: “Can we agree the scandal is that Indianapolis is up ten?”
response: “Can we agree,” Jack says, “that the scandal is Indianapolis is up ten?”

The room groans at him from every direction, Remy from under the cap, Celeste in a whisper, Josie from under the table. Lena puts her face in her hand. Clovis laughs, a big Breaux Bridge laugh that goes on, until Aints III lifts his head off the rug and joins in, a long low howl at the ceiling with the bandana going up and down on it.
“*Bon*,” says Mémère, to both of them, and the dog stops.
Aints III puts his chin back down across Jack’s ankle with a sigh for all of Indianapolis.

s07.slug: SUNDAY · 6:40 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT ROOM — THE FLOOR
body: The first quarter runs out, and Clovis takes his visor off his knee and puts it back on his head, which in this house means the second quarter. By now it is dark on Dupre Street, and the front room is lit by Miami. The green of the field is on every face in the house. Mémère’s lamp makes a yellow island by the window, and through the screen door the porch light is on over the back of Tony’s head. It has not turned around since the coin toss. The Colts are up ten. Twenty-some people are sitting in that ten like a waiting room.

Early in the quarter the Saints get as far as they can get and send out Hartley, and the house watches a forty-six-yard field goal in total silence, the twins’ faces pressed to the rug under the dining table to see it between the chair legs. It goes through. 10–3. Remy kisses the TV screen, and Celeste whispers him off it.

The next time they have the ball they take it the length of the field the slow way, eight yards and six and a first down, Brees throwing short to whoever is open, the room calling out the yard line like bingo. Somewhere around the twenty Lena comes up off the rug onto her knees. Somewhere around the ten she sits back on her heels. Inside the five she sits down again, and back, and her back comes to rest against his shins, where he is sitting against the couch with his knees up. He doesn’t move them.

First and goal. Second. A slip on third down that brings Clovis up out of his chair with both hands on his head. On fourth down at the one nobody comes out to kick, and the whole house understands it together and gets to its feet, Kevin included. Lena doesn’t get up. Her hand comes back over her shoulder without her eyes leaving the screen and finds his wrist where it hangs off his knee, and takes hold, hard, all five fingers. The ball goes into the middle. The middle doesn’t move.

Clovis’s hat is on the floor. Aints III gets up and goes and lies down under the dining table with the twins, who make room. Mémère crosses herself backward, forehead, heart, right shoulder, left, stops, looks at her hand, and does it again correctly with her mouth set. Lena’s fingers come off his wrist one at a time, as if she has only now noticed where they got to, and go back to her lap.
The Colts take it on their own one and run three times into the middle of the field and punt, and the room sits down by degrees and starts, very quietly, to hope again.

Tess gets up from the floor by the television with Lucille on her shoulder, steps over Josie’s feet and around Margot’s footstool, and comes down the room to him. She bends and puts her daughter into his arms over the top of her sister’s head.
“Hold her for me,” she says. “You know how.”

She goes off up the hall toward the kitchen and does not come back. Lucille is asleep in the black-and-gold cap with the fleur-de-lis on top, and she smells of milk and warm wool, and when he gets her into the crook of his left arm her mouth works at a dream and gives up. Lena reaches up without turning around. She finds the baby’s fist by feel, opens it with her thumb, and puts one finger in it, and the fist closes, and Lena puts her head back against his knee and watches the two-minute warning like that.

body.text: Something soft lands on his shoulder from above: a burp cloth, white flannel with ducks on it. “Don’t make it a thing, fireman,” says Laney, from the couch.

body: He turns his head once, to put the Barq’s down on the end of the coffee table out of the baby’s way, and sees the far end of the couch. Laney has a hand on Theo’s knee and the knuckles of it are white. Theo has his eyes on the television and his mouth shut so hard it has gone small and straight. Their eyes go to each other over Jack’s head and over Lena’s, and come away, and Jack catches the tail of it and turns back to the game.

Thirty-some seconds left in the half, and the Saints get the ball back near midfield and move it just far enough. Hartley again, from forty-four, with time for nothing after. It goes through as the clock runs out. 10–6. The room sits down all at once on everything in it that will hold a person, and Clovis picks his hat up off the rug and puts it back on.
On her footstool Margot uncaps a pen and writes in her notebook, steadily, without hurry, and says it as she writes: “Field note. The punishment is being served willingly.”
“*Margot,*” says Laney.

Lena is already up. She takes her finger back from the baby, and Tess comes down the room for Lucille, and Lena stacks the empty bowls off the rug and the coffee table onto her hip and carries them back through the house to the kitchen, and the back door bangs.

On the television the field is full of people in the dark wheeling a stage on, and then the lights come up all over it, red and white, and two old Englishmen at the middle of it with a band behind them, and the first guitar comes out of the set at a volume Celeste does not allow in this house and allows tonight.
“Who Dat,” Remy says from the arm of the couch, with his cap over his heart. “Who Are You. It’s the same question.”

Over Jack’s head Celeste leans down out of her corner of the couch. She sets a plate of gumbo on the cushion by his ear, rice in the middle, a paper napkin tucked under the rim, and with her foot she slides the empty Igloo across the rug till it touches his knee.
“Baby. Ice. Again,” she whispers. “And Tony hasn’t eaten since the anthem. He won’t come in for it.”

choices.text: Take Tony a plate.
Take the cooler out back.

s07b.slug: SUNDAY · 7:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE SHED — ICE
body: The back steps go down into a yard that has gone cold and blue. The kitchen window is open its crack over the sink, and it throws a yellow square onto the grass and the halftime show out with it, drums and a stadium and a guitar chopping away at the same few chords. The big boil pot is still upside down on the picnic table where it was this afternoon. The burner is a black ring on its stand. At the back of the lot the shed is a white shape under the oak, its door standing open, and out of the door comes a cold white light from low down, and Lena is in the light.

She has pushed the sleeves of her shirt up past the elbows, the way she does, and she is bent over the chest freezer just inside the shed door with both arms in it to the elbow. The freezer’s own bulb comes up on her face from below. Her bowls are stacked in the concrete tub by the shed, rinsed and upside down.
The shed’s light is off.

He puts the cooler down on the grass at her feet with the lid open. She doesn’t look up. She hands him a bag of ice without a word, and he puts it in, and she hands him another. They are frozen to each other at the corners, and the third one won’t come, so she brings it up out of the freezer two-handed and cracks it down on the freezer’s rim, hard, and the ice inside the plastic goes to gravel, and she hands it to him.
“Mama buys ice like she’s laying out a wake,” she says.

Each time she hands a bag across, her fingers are on the plastic where his have to go, and they meet on it, cold on cold, and part, and meet again on the next one. The grass is wet and cold through the leather of his boots, and two yards over somebody’s grandmother is out on her own back steps with a cordless phone, in French, with *fourth down* in English in the middle of it.

The cold comes up out of the freezer in a slow fog and goes over the rim onto both their hands. It is cold enough out here that what they say shows. The shed door drifts toward him on its hinges in no wind and drifts back, and he puts the side of his boot against it.

body.text: Lena goes in again, down to the bottom, after the last of it. “You didn’t say it,” she says, into the freezer. “In the car. About her mother.”
He holds the cooler. “It wasn’t mine.”

“I know.” She comes up with a bag of ice against her chest, and frost on the dark hair of her forearms, and puts it in the cooler on top of the others. “That’s the one thing either of us did right in New Mexico.”

Lena straightens with the last bag against her chest and frost on the dark hair of her forearms, and looks at his boot on the shed door, holding it. “You know about the doors,” she says, and puts the ice in the cooler.

Lena straightens with the last bag against her chest and frost on the dark hair of her forearms, and looks at his boot on the shed door, holding it. “Daddy hung that door,” she says, and puts the ice in the cooler.

body: Through the kitchen window the band crashes into the next song, and the stadium in Miami sings along.

choices.text: “It was the worst thing I’ve ever said to anybody. The movie.”
choices.cue: Lena will hold on to that.
choices.key: By the freezer in the shed you told Lena the movie line was the worst thing you’ve ever said to anybody.
response: “It was the worst thing I’ve ever said to anybody,” he says. “The movie.”
Lena stands there with her red hands hanging at her sides and looks at him, the freezer light on half her face, for as long as it takes the band to get through a verse.
“I know,” she says. And then, with her chin up: “It was very good, though.”

It almost gets both of them. It gets her: one laugh, short, out of her nose into the cold, with sound to it. It nearly gets him. She shuts the freezer. The light goes off it. They take the cooler up by its two handles, one each, and carry it across the yard and up the back steps, and through the screen door the halftime show is ending on one long chord with a stadium roaring over the top of it.

choices.text: Take the ice out of her hands. Hers are freezing.
choices.key: By the freezer in the shed you took the ice out of Lena’s hands and held them till they were warm.
response: Her hands are red to the wrist and stiff, and when she reaches into the freezer again he takes the bag out of them and drops it in the cooler, and takes her hands in his.

They are colder than the ice. He holds them, the two of them together inside his two, and she lets him. Nothing gets said. In the kitchen window the drummer comes in under the guitar, and the song goes on to its end, and the whole time her fingers are getting their feeling back against his palms, he can feel it happen, the stiffness going out of them knuckle by knuckle, until they are only cold.

She takes them back. She shuts the freezer, and the light goes off it, and she bends for her handle of the cooler. They carry it up the back steps together, through the yellow of the kitchen window and into the kitchen light.

choices.text: “Kevin’s going to want a count.”
choices.key: By the freezer in the shed you told Lena that Kevin would want a count. She said twelve. There were five.
response: Lena looks down into the cooler. There are five bags in it, one of them in pieces.
“Twelve,” she says.
“Twelve’s the count,” he says. “Five’s the ice. Kevin can take the other seven on faith.”

“Then he can say a decade on them.” She shuts the freezer on her side of the argument, and the light goes off, and the yard goes back to the kitchen window. They lift the cooler by its two handles and carry it up the back steps and down the hall, past Mémère’s armchair, where Mémère looks into it as it goes by and says something short in French that Lena won’t translate.

s07t.slug: SUNDAY · 7:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH — TONY
body: The cold has come down on the porch while the game was on. It is the first night in New Orleans that feels like February, damp and close, the oak over the street black against the sky, and every porch on Dupre Street is lit. On every one there is a man, or two men, in a chair, with a radio on the rail. The halftime show comes out of the house behind Jack through the screen door, a stadium of drums and a big voice going up, and a few houses down somebody has a window open on the same thing a half second behind.

Tony has his kitchen chair tipped back against the wall under the window and his feet up on the rail beside the radio, a battered silver transistor with a coat hanger for an antenna, turned down so far the WWL halftime men are a murmur of grown men being reasonable. Ferd’s folding chair beside him is empty. Ferd’s cooler isn’t.
Jack holds out the plate.
Tony looks at it, and up at him. “She send you?”
“Yes, sir.”

“Course she did.” He brings his feet down off the rail and the chair down on all four legs and takes the plate on his knees. He eats the first spoonful slowly, like a man reading a contract to the bottom, and nods to himself. He looks up past the porch light at the porch ceiling, painted pale blue.
“Ten–six, Lord,” he says, at no more than his ordinary volume. “I’m not complaining. I’m noting it.” He eats. “We had a deal. I been carrying the account since I was in short pants.”
Jack sits down on the top step with his back against the post.
“Lena tell you about the bag?”
“She did.”

“She tells it wrong.” Tony points the spoon at him. “She tells it like I brought it from home. I paid a dollar for that bag. Man in our section, nineteen-eighty, going up and down the row with a stack of Schwegmann’s bags over his arm like a waiter, a dollar apiece. A *dollar*. Celeste cut the eyeholes in it with her sewing scissors. She had them in her purse. She was twenty years old.” He shakes his head at the street. “Who brings scissors to a football game? I married her for that. One and fifteen, we went. I wore the bag for the last six. This is the forty-third season. Forty-three, son.”

Down the block a man on a porch yells something about the second half at the street, and somebody else yells back, *Who dat*, and somebody else answers, and it goes down the street porch to porch and dies out by Esplanade.
Tony eats. With his spoon he points at the floor of the porch, the rail, the steps. “We put this porch back in ’07. My brothers and me. I wanted the steps steep.”

Jack looks down them. From the top step they drop away under the porch light into the dark like a ladder into a ship’s hold, and the sidewalk at the bottom of them is broken up into slabs by the roots of the oak.

body.text: “Your girl in Canada,” Tony says, eating. “She a Colts fan?”
Jack looks at him. Tony goes on eating. “Today,” Jack says.

“Good,” Tony says. “Somebody ought to be.” And that is all of that. He scrapes the edge of the plate for rice and asks Jack, in the same voice, whether Ohio has ever produced a kicker worth a damn, and listens to the answer.

body: The gumbo goes down. Tony is quiet for a stretch, chewing, watching the street, the radio murmuring at his elbow.
“She don’t sleep in cars,” he says.
A spoon of gumbo.
“Two hours to Breaux Bridge on Christmas Eve, two hours back Christmas night, since she was in the car seat. Eyes open. Counting cows.”
He looks at the radio. Jack looks at the radio too. On the WWL halftime the men are going over the fourth down at the one again, and agreeing with each other about it at some length.

choices.text: “Thank you for having us, sir. All six.”
choices.key: At halftime you took Tony a plate on the porch and thanked him for having all six of you. You’re not company, he said.
response: Tony looks at him over the plate.
“You’re not company, son,” he says. “Company don’t get the paddle.”

He scrapes the last of the rice into the spoon and eats it, and hands Jack the plate, empty, with the spoon in it, and Jack takes it. Tony turns the transistor on the rail until its face is square on his again, tips his chair against the wall, and shuts his eyes.

choices.text: “In Youngstown we’d have to win one first.”
choices.key: At halftime you took Tony a plate on the porch and told him that in Youngstown they’d have to win one first. He had to put the plate down.
response: It goes into Tony slowly and comes out all at once. He laughs, a huge, helpless, wheezing laugh from the middle of the big body, and the gumbo starts to go over the edge of the plate, and he has to bend down and set it on the boards of the porch beside the chair and put his hands on his knees and laugh into the street. A man two porches down leans out to see what’s funny.
“*Browns*,” Tony tells him, wiping his eyes, and the man nods and goes back in.
Tony picks the radio up off the rail and holds it to his ear like a shell. The plate stays on the boards by his foot.

choices.text: Ask him what he’ll do if they win.
choices.key: At halftime you took Tony a plate on the porch and asked what he’ll do if they win. Cry on somebody’s car, he said.
response: “If they win,” Jack says. “What will you do?”
Tony doesn’t have to think about it. He has been thinking about it, by the sound of it, most of his life.
“Cry on somebody’s car,” he says.
He goes back to his gumbo, and turns the radio on the rail until its face is square on his. He jerks his chin at the door. “Go on in. You’re on the floor.”

s08.slug: SUNDAY · 7:30 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT ROOM — AMBUSH

body.text: When he comes in off the porch the teams are already lining up for the second half, and Lena is back on the floor before him, cross-legged in the middle of the rug. The cooler is full at her mother’s feet. There are chips of ice in her hair from the shed, little and bright, and one of them is melting down the side of her neck into her collar. She doesn’t look round. She moves her knee, and the middle of the rug is his again.
body.else: They come in up the hall with the cooler between them, a handle each, and set it down at Celeste’s feet, and sit down on the rug where they were, his knees up, her back against his shins, while in Miami the teams come out for the second half. Lena wipes her wet hands on the knees of his jeans, both of them, thoroughly, and goes on watching the screen.

body: The room gets up for the kickoff, because the room gets up for everything now. Celeste stands at her corner of the couch. Remy stands on the arm of it. Clovis is on his feet by the door with his hat in both hands, and Mémère is up out of her armchair on Kevin’s arm with the beads going. Lena comes up off the rug, and he comes up behind her, and through the screen door Tony’s chair scrapes on the porch boards as Tony gets up out there too, with his back to it all.

On the television the Saints’ punter, who does their kickoffs, sets the ball on the tee at his own thirty and backs away from it and stands with his hand up. The Colts are spread across their half of the field in blue, waiting for it to come to them. He comes up to the ball.

He doesn’t kick through it. He comes down on the top of it, and the ball squirts off the tee sideways, short and low and ugly along the grass, end over end, and takes a bad hop, and jumps up at the Colts’ front line at about the height of a man’s chest.
Somebody in the room says, “What —”
Lena turns round. She turns her back on the television and puts her face in his shoulder, hard, and both her fists go into the front of his shirt.

The ball goes off a blue jersey’s hands, and up, and down into a lot of legs, and the legs come together over it, and then there is no ball, only a heap of men in white and blue at about the forty, and more of them coming in from both sides and diving onto the top of it. Mémère’s beads stop. By the door Clovis puts his hand over Aints III’s eyes.

And then it goes on. The officials get to the heap and start pulling men off it by the backs of their jerseys, one at a time, and each man comes up out of the pile pointing, a white arm one way and a blue arm the other, both of them sure. The camera goes in close on the bottom of it and finds only elbows. The men in the booth don’t know. The men on the radio, through the screen, don’t know, and Tony is shouting at them to tell him. *Tell me. Tell me. TELL ME.* In the front room on Dupre Street twenty-some people and a dog stand with their mouths open and make no sound at all, and in the quiet Jack can hear the box fan going round up in the attic, where it has been going since last night.
“Tell me,” Lena says, into his shirt. “Jack. Tell me.”

He can’t. He has his hand on the back of her head, and the pencil through her hair is against his palm, and he’s watching a man in a striped shirt on his knees with both arms in the bottom of a heap of men, feeling around in there.
The striped shirt stands up. He points.

The graphic comes up in the corner of the screen, SAINTS BALL, and out of the bottom of the pile a man in white comes up with it in his arms, and a name goes across the bottom of the picture, REIS, and the house on Dupre Street goes up like a shook bottle.

Remy comes off the arm of the couch onto the coffee table, and the coffee table holds. Clovis’s hat goes up and hits the ceiling fan. Celeste’s whisper comes up out of her for the first time all weekend at its real size, and its real size is a scream. Tony is at the screen door with his radio in one hand and the other hand spread on the screen, howling through it at the room he won’t come into, and the twins come out from under the dining table on their knees, and Aints III is barking at everything, and on the floor by the television Lucille wakes up in her black-and-gold cap and is furious with every one of them.

In the noise Lena comes up out of his shoulder. She’s up on her toes, laughing into his collar, both fists still full of his shirt, and his arms are round her, one hand between her shoulder blades and the other low on her back where her shirt has come untucked, and the side of her face is against his neck, wet. His breath has gone out of him and not come back. His face is hot, and getting hotter, and it comes up into him like the heat off a pour in the stories the old Sheet & Tube men tell after Mass at St. Brigid’s: on your face first, and your eyes shut after. A piece of her hair has come down and is caught in the stubble along his jaw, and it smells of the cold out by the shed and of Mémère’s kitchen, and every time she laughs it pulls.

choices.text: Hold on.
choices.key: At the onside kick to open the second half, when the house went up, you held on to Lena a second longer than the room did.
response: All over the room people are letting go of each other, Remy of Clovis, Celeste of the couch, Kevin of Mémère’s elbow. He keeps her. Her laugh runs down into his collar and stops there.

choices.text: Let go first.
choices.key: At the onside kick to open the second half, when the house went up, you let go of Lena first. Her hand stayed in your shirt.
response: He takes his hands off her back and puts them down at his sides. Hers doesn’t move. She stands there on the rug in the uproar with her face turned to the television and a fistful of his shirt front still in her hand, and keeps it.

choices.text: Lift her off the floor.
choices.key: At the onside kick to open the second half, when the house went up, you lifted Lena off the floor. Remy yelled brother-in-law, and the room roared it.
response: He gets his arms round her and lifts, and her socks come up off Mémère’s rug, and she shrieks right in his ear. From the top of the coffee table Remy points his beer at the two of them and roars, “BROTHER-IN-LAW!” and the room roars it with him, at the television, at the dog, at Miami.

s08a.slug: SUNDAY · 7:32 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — THE SINK

body.text: He sets her down. Remy has moved on to the dog.
Her hand comes out of his shirt. She smooths the place where it was with two quick strokes, and turns back to Miami.
He lets go when the room does, a second after.

body: He goes for ice.

The cooler is full of it, at Celeste’s feet, and he steps round it on the way. Up the hall, past the bedrooms with their doors open on dark beds and coats, past the bathroom with a jelly jar of toothbrushes on the sink, into the kitchen, where every light is on.

It’s too bright in here after the front room. The overhead and the light over the stove both burn on an empty room: Mémère’s big pot on the back burner with the lid cocked and her spoon laid across it, the gumbo gone down dark and low; a stack of bowls in the drainer; the paper towels; the Community Coffee can; a calendar from Broussard’s Seafood on the side of the refrigerator, still on January. The window over the sink is open its crack on the yard. Out there it’s black, and the shed is a pale shape at the back of the black, under the oak.
He puts both hands on the edge of the sink.

It’s an old double sink, white enamel over cast iron, chipped down to the black at the corner by the faucet, and the edge of it is cold and still wet from somebody’s bowls. He grips it. He turns on the cold tap, and the water comes down hard into the empty side and roars in the iron, and he doesn’t put his hands under it. He stands with his hands on the edge of the sink and watches the water go down the drain.
Up the hall the front room is roaring at every yard. A pass, and the house yells. A run, and the house yells. Mémère says something in French, sharp, and the room laughs.

His knuckles have gone white along the edge of the enamel. He looks at them. In the window glass over the sink, laid over the dark yard by the kitchen light, there is a man with his head down and his hands on a sink, and he doesn’t look at the man. He looks past him, at the shed.

He shoves at the sink, once, with both arms, as if it might move. It’s cast iron, bolted into a house Tony and his brothers put back together by hand, and it doesn’t. The water goes on running. He stands with his arms locked and his head down between his shoulders and lets the water run, and the edge of the enamel cuts a line across the heels of both his hands, and he leaves them there till it hurts, and longer.
From the front room, over everything, over the television and Remy and the dog, her voice:
“They’re *driving*, Youngstown —”
He turns the water off. He wipes his hands down the front of his jeans and goes back up the hall.

They are driving. He gets back to the rug in time to see Brees throw short, nothing to it, to Pierre Thomas out on the edge of things, and Thomas turn up the field with three men in front of him and follow them into the end zone, sixteen yards, while the front room comes apart. 13–10, and for the first time in forty-three seasons the Saints are ahead in a Super Bowl.
Mémère puts her beads to her lips. “*Merci*,” she says, to the ceiling.

The Colts take the kickoff and go the length of the field straight back at them, the same straight line as the first quarter, Manning at the line with his hands going, and Addai runs it in from the four, and it’s 17–13 Colts, and the room sits down hard on everything in it, the arm of the couch, the footstool, the dog.

Late in the quarter Hartley trots out again, from forty-seven this time. Under the dining table Josie has both hands over Jude’s eyes, and Jude has both of his over hers. It goes through with room to spare. 17–16.
Lena is up on her knees on the rug for the kick. When it’s through she sits back down, and back, into him, and settles there against his chest as if she’d never got up.

s09.slug: SUNDAY · 8:20 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT ROOM — THE FOURTH QUARTER
body: The fourth quarter comes on with the house on its feet, and doesn’t let it sit back down. Through the screen door the porch light is on over Tony’s head, and up and down Dupre Street every open door has the same green field in it, and the same quiet.

Early in the quarter the Colts stall and send out their old kicker from fifty-one yards. Mémère closes her eyes. The ball goes up, and drifts, and goes wide, and the house yells at it the length of its fall.
Clovis takes his hat off and holds it to his chest. “God bless that man’s family,” he says, with real feeling.

The Saints get the ball back on the long side of the field and go down it short, short, short: a pass to the flat, a pass over the middle, a pass to the flat again, Brees throwing to whoever is standing still, and the room stops calling it out and only breathes in when the ball goes up and out when it comes down. At the two he throws to the tight end in the end zone, the big one, Shockey, and Shockey has it, and the house goes up for it, and Remy kisses the television again, and this time Celeste lets him. 22–17.

They go for two. Brees throws to Lance Moore in a crowd at the goal line, and Moore goes down with the ball stretched out in front of him, and on the way down a Colt knocks it out of his hands, and the official waves it off. Incomplete. The yell turns over in the room halfway out and dies.
On the sideline Payton has a red flag in his hand, and he throws it.

And so they wait. The referee goes over to the replay booth at the side of the field and puts his head into the hood, and on the television the same two seconds of Lance Moore go by forward and backward and forward again in slow motion, the ball in his hands over the line, the ball not over the line, the ball over the line, while the front room stands with its hands on its head. Mémère has the beads in both fists, knuckles white, going at a pace Kevin has stopped trying to match.
Lena is up on her knees on the rug with her hands clasped in front of her mouth. “I have never asked You for one thing about football,” she says, with her eyes shut. “Not one thing.”
“*Ah, non?*” says Mémère, without opening hers.
“Not *this year*.”
Celeste leans down the couch toward Kevin on his dining chair, low, the house’s business voice. “Kevin, baby. You’re the medical authority. Can Tony have another Sazerac?”
Kevin doesn’t take his eyes off the hood. “Respectfully, not until the ruling.”

The referee comes out from under it. He walks out to the middle of the field and turns on his microphone, and the house goes silent to hear him, and whatever he says, the official behind him has both arms straight up over his head, and the house can’t hear the rest for itself. 24–17. Aints III howls, and Clovis howls with him.

Then Manning gets the ball back with five and a half minutes on the clock and starts down the field the way he has been going down it all night, in a straight line, short, sure, his hands going at the line, and the room stands up and stays up. Through the window Jack can see Tony on the porch on his feet with the transistor held up a foot from his face, shouting at it to do something about Indianapolis.
Somewhere around midfield Lena’s hand is in his.

He doesn’t know which of them did it. He doesn’t look down at it, and she doesn’t. They stand on the rug with their fingers laced, and their eyes on Miami, and her thumb going back and forth across the back of his hand, over the knuckles, every time Manning takes the snap.
Third down. Manning drops back and throws for Wayne, short, and a Saint has stepped into the space between them, and takes the ball in stride, and is gone.
Theo sees it first. From the far end of the couch, hoarse, a full second ahead of the house:
“*PORTER* —”

And then everybody. Tracy Porter goes down the sideline with the ball in his arm and no one in blue within ten yards of him, past the forty, the thirty, Manning himself coming across at him and going down on the grass too late, and the twins are screaming, and Clovis is screaming, and Celeste is screaming with Remy on her back, and Laney has both arms round Theo’s neck and is screaming straight into his chest, and Porter crosses the goal line and keeps going, and on the screen the clock in the corner reads 3:12.
Through the window, on the porch, under the light, Tony is down on his knees on the boards with his hands over his face and the radio in his lap.
Lena has turned to Jack with both his hands in hers and is shaking them, up and down, hard, shouting something at him he can’t hear and doesn’t need to.

Hartley kicks the extra point. 31–17. The last three minutes the room stands for. The Colts come back down the field anyway, because they’re the Colts, all the way to the shadow of the goal line, and the house holds them there, every soul in it, Mémère with her beads up in the air like a fist. On fourth down the pass falls on the grass, and it’s the Saints’ ball, and Brees comes out and takes the snap and goes down on one knee with it, and the clock runs down, and the room counts it with the television, in English and in French.
Zero.
Saints 31, Colts 17.

On the television there is confetti coming down over the field in Miami, and in the middle of it Brees is standing with his baby son in his arms, a little boy in a pair of big ear protectors, looking up at all of it falling.
On the floor by the television Tess holds Lucille up to the screen with both hands under her arms, so she can see.

choices.text: Find Mémère first.
choices.key: When the clock hit zero you found Mémère first. She took your face in both hands and said something in French, and Lena wouldn’t translate it.
response: She is still in front of her armchair with Kevin’s arm under her elbow, very small in the uproar, and he gets across the room to her through Remy and the coffee table and the dog. She looks up at him. She puts the beads in Kevin’s hand and takes Jack’s face in both of hers, dry, cool, strong, and pulls it down to her level, and says something to him in French, low and fast and a good deal of it.
“*Bon garçon*” is the only part he gets. Across the room Lena has seen it, and she shakes her head at him: she isn’t translating that.

Mémère lets go of his face and pats it. Remy and Clovis come and take her by an elbow each, and she lets them, and the front room picks the two of them up with everyone else and carries them out the front door.

choices.text: Find Kevin.
choices.key: When the clock hit zero you found Kevin. He took your pulse, for the record.
response: Kevin is on his feet by Mémère’s chair with the rosary still wound round his hand, and when Jack gets to him he takes Jack’s wrist without a word and puts two fingers on the inside of it, and looks at his watch.
Kevin counts. The house goes off around them.
“You’re fine,” Kevin says. He keeps the fingers there. He looks up from the watch at Jack’s face. “You’re *not* fine.”
Celeste is at the door with it hooked open on her hip, shooing the room through it with both hands like chickens. “Out. Out. Everybody out,” she whispers, and everybody goes.

choices.text: Out the door with Remy.
choices.key: When the clock hit zero you went out the front door with Remy before anybody, and the whole street came with you.
response: Remy is already going, and Jack goes with him, through the screen door so hard the spring sings, past Tony on his knees, and Remy reaches down on the way and takes the radio out of his father’s lap and holds it up over his head with the WWL man’s voice coming out of it cracked and gone. They take the steep steps three at a time, Remy riding the rail for the bottom half, into Dupre Street, and every door on the block opens at once behind them and lets out everybody inside it.

choices.text: Find Celeste.
choices.key: When the clock hit zero you found Celeste. She kissed you on the forehead and sent you out the door with everybody else.
response: She is at her end of the couch with both hands over her mouth, and the whisper has gone back down to wherever she keeps it. When he gets to her she takes her hands down and takes his head in them by the ears, the way you’d take a pot off the stove, and kisses him once on the forehead, hard.
“Go on, baby,” she whispers, and turns him by the shoulders toward the door, where the front room is already going.

s10.slug: SUNDAY · 9:05 PM · N. DUPRE STREET — THE STREET
s10.music: Dirty Dozen Brass Band — “My Feet Can’t Fail Me Now”
body: The first thing is the noise. It comes out of every door on Dupre Street at once, out of the screen doors and the open windows and down the steep steps, and it brings the people with it: men in jerseys with their arms over their heads, women with pot lids and soup spoons, a little boy on his father’s shoulders hitting a cowbell with a wrench, a grandmother in a quilted housecoat beating a saucepan with a meat tenderizer, down into the road under every porch light on the block. A nun in a gold sweatshirt goes by on a bicycle, ringing the bell on her handlebars the length of the street. Two doors down a man has a trumpet he can’t play, and he is playing it, the first three notes of something, over and over. Out on Esplanade the car horns have started, every horn on the avenue leaning on the Who Dat. A fire truck crosses the end of the street with its lights turning and its siren going, and the men riding the back step have their helmets off and are waving them.

Over the roofs somebody sets off fireworks that, from the size of them, he has been saving since 1967. They go up green and gold over the oaks and come apart, and the smoke drifts down into the street and hangs under the branches in the porch light, powder and cigars and somebody’s grill and, under all that, something sweet off a tree in a yard he can’t see.

Halfway down the block a pickup is parked with both doors open and the radio turned up as far as it goes, a tuba walking along the bottom of a song and the horns piling in on top of it, and in front of its headlights people who were strangers at the kickoff are dancing in the road.

The Broussards are all through it. A woman in a flannel nightgown and a Brees jersey comes down off her porch in her slippers, takes Nonc Clovis’s face in both hands and kisses him on the mouth, lets go of him, and goes on up the street to find somebody else, and Clovis stands in the road with his visor in his hand. Aints III sits down on the center line, puts his head back and howls, and three houses’ worth of dogs answer him. Remy is standing on the roof of a parked Camry with both arms up, and the Camry’s owner is standing on its hood below him with both arms up, and the Camry is holding. Up on the porch somebody has put Mémère in the swing with a blanket over her knees and her beads in her lap, and people come up the steep steps one after another to kiss her, and to each of them she says *merci*. Celeste sits on the top step below her with Lucille against her shoulder, laughing and crying into the black-and-gold cap, and Lucille is awake and furious about all of it.

Tony is off the porch. He got as far as the curb. He is bent over the hood of a stranger’s car, a green Grand Am with a Mississippi plate, with his arms spread across it and his face down on the metal and his sport coat rucked up over the Brees jersey, crying with his shoulders, and the man who owns the Grand Am, in a Shockey jersey, stands over him patting him on the back in a slow, steady rhythm, and is crying too.

Jack is in the middle of the street. The Broussards’ front room came out the door behind him and went in every direction, Kevin steering Margot by the elbow, Theo carrying Laney down the steps because she had lost a shoe, the twins over the rail.
