A man he has never seen in his life has hugged him twice. A woman in gold face paint has kissed him on the ear on her way past, and somebody put a can of Abita in his hand, and somebody else took it. Up and down Dupre Street people are holding on to each other in the road under the porch lights: cousins, neighbors, strangers, a couple in matching gold wigs, two old men who got up out of their lawn chairs at the same time and haven’t let go yet, the dancers in front of the truck. He has turned around, toward the house.
She comes off the curb at a run.
She is in her socks on the asphalt, her hair coming down, the medal swinging out on its chain, and she’s in his arms before either of them thinks.

He has her up off the road and down again. Her arms are round his neck. His are round her back, and the city goes off around them, the pot lids, the horns, the fire truck coming back round the block the other way, a whistle somewhere, the trumpet. She is shaking. Her ribs go in and out against his, fast, and the back of her shirt is damp under his hands, and her ear is cold against his cheek and the rest of her is hot. Her socks are soaked from the road. Somewhere in it she has stepped up onto his boots to get out of the wet, and she stands there.
She leans back far enough to see his face. She keeps her hands on his arms to do it.
The light off her mother’s porch is on her. Her face is wet to the chin. She’s laughing up at him with the hair across one eye, a laugh he can hear over the trumpet, and then the laugh stops.

Her face stays turned up to his. Her lips are parted, and nothing comes out of them. Over the South Side in December, the hour before snow, the sky goes like this: low and close and yellow-gray, the streetlights on at four in the afternoon, the air gone still, and nothing falling yet. Her face has that sky in it.

There is gold paint on her cheekbone, a fleur-de-lis some stranger thumbed onto her between the porch and the curb, half of it gone now into the front of his shirt. Over her shoulder the Camry’s owner has climbed down off his hood to kiss his wife on the sidewalk, and two strangers in Saints wigs are kissing against a lamppost, and the woman in the nightgown has found somebody else.

Behind her a man is beating a saucepan with a spoon. The trumpet two doors down finds a fourth note at last, and loses it. His hands are open on her back, and they stay open. Her hands stay on his arms.

choices.text: “Lena.”
choices.key: In the street after the game, with the whole city going off, Lena came off the curb into your arms. You said her name, and nothing after it.
response: “Lena,” he says.
Her name, and nothing after it. She puts her hand up to his face, cold from the street, and holds it there, and doesn’t answer it.

choices.text: Say nothing. Hold on.
choices.key: In the street after the game, with the whole city going off, Lena came off the curb into your arms. You didn’t say anything. You held on.
response: He says nothing. He holds on, and the dancers from in front of the truck come down the road in a line with their handkerchiefs going and split around the two of them and close up again on the other side.

choices.text: “Who dat.”
choices.key: In the street after the game, with the whole city going off, Lena came off the curb into your arms. You said: Who dat. She said it back, into your collar.
response: “Who dat,” he says.
Her face goes into his neck, wet, and she says it back into his collar: “Who *dat*.”

s10a.slug: SUNDAY · 9:15 PM · N. DUPRE STREET — THE HOOD OF A BUICK

body.text: Her hand is still on his face when Tony gets there.

body: He comes across the road from the Grand Am with his face wet and his sport coat open and the Brees jersey dark at the collar, and he doesn’t slow down for either of them. He takes Jack round the middle in both arms and lifts him clean off Dupre Street, so that Jack’s boots hang over the asphalt. He smells of rye and bitters and somebody else’s cigar. Into Jack’s ear, with what four quarters of radio have left of his voice, he says it:

He sets Jack down and takes him by the back of the neck and shakes him, the way you’d shake a radio to bring the station back, and lets go to grab somebody else. Josie has Lena by the wrist. She tows her backward across the road to the steps, where Tess is reaching for her, and Clovis, and the family closes over her in the porch light.

Jack steps back out of the road to the far curb, where a maroon Buick LeSabre is parked across from the Broussards’ steps with a Saints flag in its back window. He brings both hands down on its hood. The hood booms. He puts his head back and roars at the sky over Dupre Street, at the smoke and the oaks and the dark over the roofs with no stars in it, roars till there is nothing left in his chest to do it with.

Dupre Street roars back. Every porch on the block is doing it, men pounding the hoods of cars and the posts of porches and each other, women with their heads back and their eyes shut, a city with its mouth open at the sky, and his is one more. He brings his hands down on the hood again, harder, and the Buick’s alarm goes off, whooping, and the street cheers the alarm.

When he straightens up off the hood, Theo and Laney are at the bottom of the Broussards’ steps across the road. Laney has Theo by both lapels of his good coat and is shaking him, hard, and Theo is letting her; his head goes back and forth with it, and the iPhone in his hand is filming the sidewalk. Her mouth is going a mile a minute. Neither of them is watching the iPhone. Their eyes go to the Buick, and to the steps, and back to the Buick, and Laney shakes him harder.

Kevin is out in the middle of the road with his BlackBerry to one ear and a finger in the other, dialing. The network gives him nothing, and nothing again, and on the ninth or tenth try it gives him something. “Clare,” he says. “Clare. It’s Kevin. From Louisiana.” A small voice in the BlackBerry says something back. He holds the phone up over his head, out to the pot lids and the horns and the Buick, and brings it back down. “Can you hear it? Clare, that’s — that’s *all of it*.” He turns in the road with the phone at his ear, and his eyes come round to Jack at the Buick, and go on across the street to Lena on her mother’s steps, and come back.
“Hold on,” Kevin says into the phone. “Everyone’s healthy.”
Margot, kissed on the cheek in passing by a stranger in a Brees jersey, stands in the road with her notebook in her coat pocket and doesn’t take it out.
From the Broussards’ steps Remy finds Jack across the road and throws both arms up. “*Brother-in-law!*” The crowd in front of the truck takes him, and he goes into it dancing.
Nonc Clovis goes past with the nightgown woman’s lipstick on his mouth and Aints III under one arm, looking up the block the way she went.

Jude comes along the curb with a pot lid under his arm. He is thirteen, in a Saints jersey that reaches his knees, and so far he has communicated with Jack entirely by eating things in front of him. He stops. He looks up.
“Who dat,” Jude says, and goes on down the curb, hitting the pot lid with his fist.
Celeste comes across the road last, without the baby. She stops beside him at the Buick, with its alarm going, and puts her hand on his arm.
“Bring them home, baby,” she says, in her whisper, and under the alarm it reaches him anyway.
She isn’t looking at him when she says it. She is looking across the street, at the steps, at Lena.

In his jeans the RAZR has found nothing since the two-minute warning. Every phone in the city is trying at once, and the network has given up and gone out into the street with everybody else. It buzzes against his hip anyway.

body: Pop.

Jack takes it across the road. Tony is back at the Grand Am with the man in the Shockey jersey, the two of them leaning on it like a bar. Jack holds the phone out. Tony takes it in his big hand and holds it at arm’s length under the streetlight, and reads it with his lips moving, and lays it face-up on the hood of the stranger’s car, carefully. He climbs up on the Grand Am’s bumper, and the man in the Shockey jersey steadies him by the belt.
“His *daddy*,” Tony tells Dupre Street, with an arm flung out at Jack. “In *Ohio*.”

And Dupre Street, which has never heard of Frank Costigan, cheers him: the porches, the truck, the dancers in its headlights, the woman in the nightgown from halfway up the block. The man in the Shockey jersey hands Jack back his phone and shakes his hand, and somebody else shakes it, and somebody else, and his palms are still stinging from the Buick’s hood, both of them, to the wrist.

journal.title: Celeste Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s mother. A nurse — she came to the door in scrubs. Gives her orders in a whisper. Saturday night she was in the door when I came up her steps with Lena asleep, and she didn’t ask me one thing. Sunday she ran eleven people through one bathroom in a whisper. Ice, baby. In the street after the game, with the whole city yelling, she said to me: Bring them home, baby.

journal.title: Tony Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s father. Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Twenty-eight years in the same seats. Held the phone up to the kitchen radio for the whole second half while we lost him at every curve on Highway 1. Wes told him there’s a Browns fan out here. Laney had him at hello. Saturday night in the side yard he put me on the paddle inside ten minutes. Sunday in the pew he told God He owes him one. He wouldn’t watch the game; he listened on the porch, on the radio, with his eyes shut. When it was over he cried face-down on the hood of a stranger’s car, and then he picked me up off the street.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Clare asked him which of us was right at Hale’s; he told her he didn’t have the information, and she said that was a very Kevin answer. He asked if my brother’s okay. Thursday night at the van he had a clipboard and a seating chart taped to the dash, and said he’s pre-med, not a switchboard. Clare came to see him off. At three in the morning he was at St. Brendan’s ahead of me. Couldn’t sleep either. At a quarter to five Osei blessed his mother’s car again. Still pretty blessed. Friday under the dinosaurs at Cabazon he told Theo and Laney to leave it alone. He checked the oil at the Arizona line. He called Clare from El Paso, like he said he would. He kept the clock the whole way: thirty-five hours and forty minutes. Sunday night in the street he got through to Clare from Louisiana on about the tenth try, like he said he would, and held the phone up so she could hear the city.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.” Asked me what it’s like in there. Went in on Holy Family Sunday — his name was on the list at the desk; he asked Ma where he’s supposed to stand. Told Danny about the hall and the Cruze, and laughed, in there. Asked if the Saints girl sent the coffee. I said yeah. Told Danny they wouldn’t lose. Three straight. His phone died in the cold and he borrowed mine. New Year’s: a ginger ale, in a glass. New Year’s: two spoons of lentils, for the money. “Pryor.” Went in to see Danny again. “Four straight.” Twelfth Night we took the lights down, and the beer fridge is ginger ale now. At the curb in Pittsburgh: call your mother when you land. She don’t sleep. Thursday he called me — him, not Ma. He put sixty dollars in my account for gas. It ain’t a question. Theo e-mailed Ma a budget, with a chart. Watch it with people, he says; that’s the whole thing. Tell the TV one Ma says Canada’s cold. Sunday night after the game his text got through when nothing else would: tell the saints girls father congratulations. I showed Tony. Tony climbed on a stranger’s bumper to tell the block, and Dupre Street cheered a man from Ohio it’s never heard of.

s11.slug: SUNDAY · 10:20 PM · N. DUPRE STREET AT ESPLANADE
body: An hour and more after the clock ran out, Dupre Street is still in the road, but it has stopped roaring and started looking for somewhere to go. Up at the corner, where it runs into Esplanade under the oaks, a band is putting itself together out of the crowd: a tuba on a big man in a hard hat with a fleur-de-lis painted on it, a snare drum on a strap, a trombone, a trumpet, and twenty people already standing in the street behind them, waiting to be told which way.

Remy comes down the Broussards’ steep steps at a run, with his Saints cap on backward and three cousins behind him in three LSU sweatshirts in three different states of repair. He flings both arms out at the river end of Esplanade, where the car horns are. “Bourbon Street, y’all. *Now*.”

Tess has Lucille out of her mother’s arms and buckled into the car seat, and Beau has the diaper bag and the keys, and they go up the block to their car with the baby swinging asleep on Beau’s arm at last, under a blanket, through all of it. The twins are sent in. Josie argues it at the screen door — “It’s the *Super Bowl*. It happens *one time* —” — and Celeste points down the hall, and Josie goes, and Jude goes after her, beating the pot lid down the hall to the kitchen.

Celeste stays at the top of the steps with her arms folded in her cardigan and looks down at the six of them on her sidewalk, and at Remy, and at the cousins. “Home by morning,” she whispers. “All of you.” It carries to the corner.

Mémère is in the swing where they put her, with the blanket over her knees and the beads in her lap. She lifts one finger off the beads at her granddaughter on the bottom step, who has Remy’s purple sweatshirt on again, the sleeves down over her hands, and is working her feet into her Justins over two soaked socks.
“Magdalena. *Attention.*”
“*Oui*, Mémère.”
The finger comes round past Lena to Jack. “*Et toi aussi.*”
He has about forty words of French, most of them off a menu, and he doesn’t need any of them for that. “Yes, ma’am.”

Lena stands and stamps her heels down into the boots, one and then the other, on the sidewalk. The gold thumbprint is still on her cheekbone, what’s left of it. She looks down Esplanade toward the river, where the horns are, and up the block at the tuba, where the snare has started, turning from one to the other with her chin up, listening. Both ways are loud.

choices.text: Down Esplanade to the Quarter with Remy.
Fall in behind the band.

s11n.slug: SUNDAY · 10:35 PM · ESPLANADE AVENUE — THE SECOND LINE
body: Under the oaks on Esplanade the streetlights come down through the leaves in pieces, and the band walks into them. It doesn’t start so much as get going: the snare first, a kid in a Saints visor rapping on the rim, and the tuba coming in underneath him, and the trombone, and a trumpet that seems to know two songs and plays both of them with total conviction.

People come down off the porches into it as it passes. A woman in a housecoat with a white handkerchief going over her head. Two boys with a cowbell. A man in his undershirt with a cast-iron skillet and a spoon, keeping the snare’s time on the bottom of the skillet. Umbrellas go up open under a sky with no rain anywhere in it, a gold one and a black one and one with ducks on it, and bob along over the heads, and the handkerchiefs are going everywhere. Remy has gone to the Quarter with three cousins and a cooler. The rest of Dupre Street is here.
Lena is in it before the first block is out. She’s dancing, and she has his hand.
“The band’s the first line,” she says, over the tuba. “We’re the second. You’re in it now.”
She pulls him in by the hand, and she doesn’t let go of it for six blocks.

The band goes three blocks toward the river, turns down a side street for no reason anybody gives, and comes back up onto Esplanade with twice the people it left with. On a porch somebody has a grill going. Under the smoke there is the sweetness again, the one from the street after the game, heavy and close, coming off a hedge in a dark yard.
“What is that?”
“Sweet olive.” She doesn’t have to look. “It blooms when it wants. February, if it feels like it.”

It is not a march, and it isn’t a dance either, not one he has the parts for. It is the street walking with its knees. The snare kid keeps them all to it. Lena goes up and down on the back of the beat, off her heels, her free hand up with the handkerchief somebody gave her, the gold on her cheekbone shining with sweat.
“It’s in the knees,” she tells him. “Bounce. Don’t stir. You’re not making roux with your feet.”
“I’m from Ohio. We don’t dance. We shift our weight at weddings.”
He tries. She watches him try for half a block and says *Lord* to the oaks. “You dance like a man carrying a ladder.”
“It’s a family ladder.”

“Your feet are in New Orleans,” she says, “and your shoulders are still in Ohio.” She reaches over with the handkerchief hand, the other one still in his, and pushes one of his shoulders down, hard, where she wants it.

Laney is up on Theo’s shoulders by the second block, with her hands in his hair, steering him by it, conducting the trombone with a go-cup. Theo’s face, under her elbows, is very calm. From up there Laney looks down at the two hands, Jack’s and Lena’s, and drums on the top of Theo’s head with her free palm, fast, and steers him out into the middle of the street to get a better look at the trombone.
“I can see Baton Rouge from up here,” Laney announces.
“You can see my scalp,” says Theo.
“It’s a beautiful scalp. I’d crown it.”

Kevin walks at the edge of it with one hand in his jacket pocket, on his rosary, the beads going through his fingers in the snare’s time. When the line shoves him up against Jack he says, “This is hella cardio,” and goes back to his decade.

Margot dances. She dances badly and in deadly earnest, elbows out, in her black coat and black tights, half a step behind the beat and gaining on it, and when Lena points at her and shrieks, Margot says, without breaking step, “I am not dancing. I’m processing in a manner consistent with local custom.”

At a light the band passes a car stopped on the red, an old Cutlass with the windows down and an old man at the wheel. He has a record going that is older than Pop, a piano rolling along under a big easy voice, and he is conducting it with one finger over the steering wheel. Jack knows the song before he can name it, and then he can: the upright in the Delgado basement, and Lena at it. Beside him she has heard it too. The hand with the handkerchief plays two bars of the left hand on the air at her hip, and on the second bar steps around a note, the dead F, which isn’t dead here, and goes back up to the beat. The light changes. The old man sits through it.

Somewhere in the fourth block, with her hand pulling him and the tuba coming up out of the street into his boots, Jack looks back down the line. It’s a block long now. It’s porches and pot lids and umbrellas and a skillet, a woman with a baby asleep in a sling, two old men with their hats in their hands, and the sidewalks behind it empty. Four thousand words, Hale said, and not one of them *liminal*. The first sentence turns up on its own.
*A second line has no audience, only people who haven’t joined yet.*
He has no pen. The only pencil within reach is the one through Lena’s hair.
From a porch with a glider on it an old woman in curlers and a Saints sweatshirt leans out over her rail. “Lena Broussard! Is that Tony’s Lena?”
“Yes, ma’am, Miss Odette!”
“Tell your mama I said hey!”
“I will!”
“Who’s that you got?”
Lena doesn’t stop dancing. She lifts their two hands up together, his and hers, and shakes them at the porch. “He’s from *Ohio*, Miss Odette!”
“Well, God *love* him,” says Miss Odette, and sits back down in her glider.

In the fifth block the hand with the handkerchief comes down and taps the snare’s time on the inside of his wrist, three times, and goes back up. It might only be the beat. He keeps walking with his knees. He doesn’t do anything back with the hand. He keeps it as still in hers as a hand can be kept and still be holding.

At the sixth corner the band stops for water. A woman comes down off her porch with a pitcher and a sleeve of Dixie cups, and the tuba player drinks three in a row, and the snare kid pours one over his own head. Lena is breathing hard. She fans herself with the handkerchief and leans her shoulder into his arm, and the heat of her comes through the sweatshirt and the Carhartt both, and she lets go of his hand. In his jeans the RAZR goes off, and on her hip hers goes off with it, both at once, the network letting go of everything it has been holding.

body: Three from Gina, in capitals. He can see her at the kitchen table on Glenwood Avenue with the TV going in the front room behind her, typing with both thumbs and her tongue out of the corner of her mouth. Pop cried. He tries to picture it and gets nothing but the back of Pop’s neck in his chair in the front room, in the light off the television, and Ma’s hand on it.
He shuts the phone on Ma’s message and puts it away.

Beside him the light of her phone is on her face. She reads whatever it is, and types back with her thumb, short, and shuts the phone and puts it away. He keeps his eyes on his own screen while she does it. She keeps hers on hers.
The tuba player hands back his cup. The snare kid shakes the water out of his hair and hits the rim twice, and the line starts to gather itself up off the curbs.

choices.text: Let her teach you the step.
choices.key: In your first second line, up Esplanade, you let Lena teach you the step. You had it for a block.
response: “Show me,” he says.

She takes both his hands and goes backward up the middle of Esplanade in front of him with the band starting again at her back. “Off the heels. Not out. *Up.* You’re not going anywhere, you’re going up. Like you’re trying not to wake the baby.” He watches her boots. He watches her knees. He gives up on watching and does it, and somewhere past the next light his feet find it, the bounce off the heels on the back of the beat, and it comes up through him into his shoulders, and he has it.
“*There* he is,” Lena says, and goes backward faster.

He has it for one block. At the corner he loses it entirely and steps on her boot, and she doesn’t let go of his hands, and the band moves off up Esplanade toward Broad with the two of them in it, her going backward and him coming after.

choices.text: Grab a stranger’s umbrella and lead the next block.
choices.key: In your first second line, up Esplanade, you grabbed a stranger’s umbrella and led a block. Lena laughed the whole way.
response: The woman ahead of them has the gold umbrella open over her head, bouncing it. Jack takes it out of her hand — “Borrowing!” — and she shrieks and lets him have it, and he gets himself up in front of the line, behind the trombone, and holds it up over his head, open, and leads.
He has no idea what he’s doing. He bounces the umbrella. He walks with his knees, more or less. Behind him a block of New Orleans follows a Browns fan up Esplanade Avenue, and seems glad to.

Lena laughs from one corner to the next, a big honk of a laugh he can hear over the tuba, the one she doesn’t do for company. At the corner the woman takes back her umbrella and kisses him on the cheek for it, and Lena comes up the line and gets her hand back into his without missing a step.

choices.text: Explain the second line to Margot as a liturgy.
choices.key: In your first second line, up Esplanade, you explained it to Margot as a liturgy. She allowed it.
response: He drops back beside Margot. “It’s a liturgy,” he tells her.
She doesn’t stop processing. “Go on.”

“Entrance procession. The band’s the ministers. The umbrellas are the processional cross. The people come off the porches, that’s the assembly. Call and response.” He points at the trumpet, which is starting its other song. “Two hymns. Same two every week. And when it gets where it’s going, everybody’s sent home.”
Margot dances half a block on it, elbows out. “You realize you’ve just annexed somebody else’s neighborhood into the Roman rite.”
“I didn’t annex it. I said it rhymes.”

“Everything rhymes with your church, Costigan. That’s the trick of a universal claim. You can hear yourself in anybody.” She gets two steps closer to the beat. “Procession, response, dismissal,” she says. “I’ll allow it.”
Margot processes on up Esplanade, a little less behind the beat than she was, and Lena comes back down the line for Jack and takes his arm.

s11q.slug: MONDAY · 12:10 AM · BOURBON STREET — THE CRUSH
body: Esplanade is two miles from Dupre Street to the river, and every porch on it is lit. The oaks close over the neutral ground, and the streetlights come down through them in pieces onto the people walking underneath, and there are a great many people, all of them going the one way, toward the river, in black and gold: families towing coolers on wheels, a man pushing his grandmother in a wheelchair with a Saints flag zip-tied to the handles, girls in gold wigs, an old man in a black blazer with a cane in one hand and a transistor radio in the other, held to his ear, though the game has been over for an hour. A goat goes by on a leash in a Brees jersey. Its owner tells anybody who asks that the goat called it in August.

“It’s the Christmas Eve crawl,” Lena says beside him, with her hands up inside the sleeves. “Everybody walking church to church all night. Except tonight it’s the one church, and Mémère’s going to hear about it.”

The damp comes up off the river to meet them. Jack gets the Browns knit out of the Carhartt’s pocket, the spare off the hook by the side door on Glenwood Avenue, and pulls it on, and Remy, walking backward at the front with his cousins, sees it and crosses himself.

Past Claiborne the avenue goes under the interstate, and the horns come back off the concrete overhead twice as loud, and up on the ramp a man has stopped his car on the shoulder to stand on its roof and wave a flag down at them.

It takes them the better part of an hour. At the bottom of Esplanade the oaks give out and the Quarter starts, and the noise that has been coming up the avenue at them the length of the walk turns out to have a source.

Bourbon Street is one car wide and wall to wall, curb to curb, balcony to balcony, as far toward Canal as he can see over the heads. Beads come down off the iron balconies in handfuls, out of the light, and hit people in the face, and the people say thank you. Somebody puts a go-cup of beer in his hand and somebody else drinks it. There’s no room to dance, so people dance from the waist up, with their arms in the air and their feet going wherever the crowd puts them. At the corners the mounted police sit their big horses above all of it, the horses in their face shields, patient as furniture. A girl in a gold wig asks one of the officers if she can kiss his horse, and he tells her she can kiss the horse, and she does, on its nose, and the crowd around her cheers the horse.

It is the gate at Lordstown at shift change in Pop’s stories, four thousand men coming out at once and the lot taking half an hour to clear, if every one of them had just been told the plant was staying open. It smells of beer on the stones, and horse, and the sweet frozen stuff out of the daiquiri machines, and cigars, and something frying on every block, and under all of it the river.

The crowd takes Lena off his elbow in the first block, and he finds her, and it takes her again. The third time, she comes back from behind him. Her arms go round his waist under the open Carhartt, and her hands lock together over his belt buckle, and her face goes in between his shoulder blades.
“Walk,” she says, into his back. “I’ve got you.”

He puts his hand back over hers. Her knuckles are cold from the walk down, and her fingers are laced tight, and under his palm they don’t move. He walks. The crowd moves them half a step and stops, and half a step, and her knees knock the backs of his, and her boots come down where his just were, and through his shirt and the sweatshirt he can feel her breathing against his back, fast from the walk, and slowing.
“Mémère’s going to ask where we went,” she says, into his back.
“Tell her church.”
“I am not lying to my grandmother the night we won the Super Bowl.”
“Tell her we were catching men. It was in the Gospel.”
Her forehead knocks against his back, once. “Father Hébert would put that in a homily.”

At every corner he looks for Luc. There are uniforms everywhere, on foot and on horseback and two of them by a cruiser with its lights going round, handing out bottles of water from a case, and none of them is Luc.

Halfway along the next block a brass band has its back to the shutters of a T-shirt shop: a tuba, a bass drum, a trombone, two trumpets, all of them young and soaked through their black T-shirts, the bell of the tuba up over the heads like something planted there. The crowd round them is singing. It knows every word. It takes Jack most of the block to place the song. It is one he knows from the oldies station in Pop’s truck, slowed down and dragged through a sousaphone until it belongs to somebody else, and once he has placed it there is no unplacing it.
Behind him, Lena is singing it too. He can’t hear her over the crowd. He can feel it, through his shirt, at the middle of his back.

He doesn’t turn around. If he turns around, her face will be right there under his, with the gold on it and her mouth still going with the words. He keeps his eyes on the tuba, and his hand on hers, and the crowd moves them half a step, and stops.

When he looks round for the others, Theo’s blond head is above the crowd a few yards back, with Laney on the end of his arm. Laney’s eyes are on Jack’s hand over Lena’s. She takes a fistful of Theo’s sleeve and says something up into his ear, and the crowd opens to one side for no reason Jack can see and closes again behind them, and they’re gone.
Kevin and Margot are not gone. They’re on the corner by a Lucky Dog cart, a hot dog the size of a canoe on bicycle wheels, and Kevin is paying the man. He hands Margot the dog in its paper.
“For science,” Kevin says.

Margot holds it out at arm’s length in the light off the cart, mustard and onions and all, and turns it to see the other side. She takes a bite. “Participant observation,” she says, with her mouth full, and takes another.

A block on, the crowd spits them out sideways into a cross street, and they fetch up on Dauphine with their backs against a pink stucco wall under a gas lamp, where there is room to stand and nothing to stand in line for. Lena’s arms come off him. She leans on the wall beside him with her head back against the stucco, getting her breath, and in his jeans and in the back pocket of hers the two phones go off at once: the bars have come back.

He can see her at the kitchen table on Glenwood Avenue with the TV going in the front room behind her, typing with both thumbs and her tongue out of the corner of her mouth. Pop cried. He tries to picture it and gets nothing but the back of Pop’s neck in his chair in the front room, in the light off the television, and Ma’s hand on it.
He shuts the phone on Ma’s message and puts it away.

Beside him the light of her phone is on her face. She reads whatever it is, and types back with her thumb, short, and shuts the phone and puts it back in her pocket. He keeps his eyes on his own screen while she does it. She keeps hers on hers.

When they go back round the corner into Bourbon the band has got through the song and into another one, and Theo and Laney have been found. They are on a second-floor balcony over the band, behind the iron lace, in the middle of a party of strangers in gold wigs whose host looks as surprised to have them as anybody, and Laney is leaning out over the rail with both arms full of beads, throwing them at the street in general and at Lena in particular. A strand lands on Lena’s head. Lena pulls it down round her neck and points up at Laney, and Laney points back. Behind her, Theo raises a go-cup to Jack with a face of perfect innocence.

Remy comes up out of the crowd at Jack’s elbow with two of the cousins, sweating under his backward cap. Ahead of them a man in a gold sequined blazer is working his way through the crush with a bottle of champagne by the neck, giving everybody a pull. Lena is up on her toes behind Jack and can’t see the band for the heads. By the band there’s a doorstep, the marble step of a shuttered shop, up out of the crowd, with only a man on it, asleep standing up against the door.

choices.text: Drink from the bottle a stranger hands you.
choices.key: On Bourbon Street after midnight you drank a stranger’s champagne straight from the bottle.
response: The man in the sequined blazer gets to them and holds the bottle out, and Jack takes it and puts his head back. It’s warm. It has gone flat toward the bottom, and it’s sweet, and the neck tastes of somebody’s lipstick and somebody else’s cigar, and the bubbles go up the back of his nose and make his eyes run. The man pounds him on the back, delighted with him.

Lena takes the bottle out of his hand. She gives it back to the stranger by the neck and makes a small cross on the man’s forehead with her thumb. “God bless you, cher,” she tells him. “Go find your people.” The man crosses himself with the bottle, and the crowd closes over him.

She doesn’t say anything to Jack about it. She wipes his mouth with the cuff of the sweatshirt, hard, as if he were one of the twins. Her arm comes round his waist again, from the side this time, her hip against his and her thumb hooked in his belt, and his mouth still sweet with it.

choices.text: Get her up on a step so she can see the band.
choices.key: On Bourbon Street after midnight you got Lena up on a step so she could see the band, and held her there.
response: “Here.” He gets her by the waist and puts her up on the doorstep beside the sleeping man, and she comes up out of the crowd with her hands on his shoulders and is, for the first time all weekend, taller than he is.

The band has gone into something he has never heard in his life, a long slow line for the trombone and the corner shouting the end of every verse back at it, and she knows every word. She sings it over his head at the tuba, with her hands on his shoulders and Laney’s beads swinging, and he stands in the crush below her with his hands on her waist and keeps her there. People shove past at his back. He doesn’t let them move him. At the end she sings the last line down at him, with her cheeks red and the light of the corner on her, and then has no breath left for anything else.
When the crowd moves she steps down off the doorstep into him and turns him round by the shoulders, and her arms go round his waist from behind again.

choices.text: Trade Remy your Browns hat for a Saints one.
choices.key: On Bourbon Street after midnight you traded Remy your Browns hat for a Saints one. A dowry, he said.
response: Jack pulls the Browns knit off his head and holds it out.

Remy looks at it under the gas lamp, brown and orange and pilled, and at Jack. He takes his Saints cap off his own head, turns it round the right way, puts it on Jack and pulls it down by the bill. He puts the Browns knit on himself. It sits on top of his head like a tea cozy.
“That’s a dowry,” Remy says.
“*Remy*,” says Lena.
“What? He got the good end. Look at this thing.” Remy rolls his eyes up at it, and the cousins applaud, and he wears it off into the crowd with his chin up.
Lena’s hand finds the back of Jack’s jeans and hooks two fingers through his belt loop, and she lets the crowd pull her along by him.

s12.slug: MONDAY · 3:40 AM · ESPLANADE AVENUE, THE NEUTRAL GROUND

body.text: They walked back up Esplanade from the river after three, the two miles of it, on feet that gave out somewhere around Claiborne and kept going anyway, and left Remy in the Quarter with three cousins and a balcony that wasn’t theirs. A few blocks short of Dupre Street, under the oaks, Lena sat down in the grass on the neutral ground and said she would get up again in a minute.
body.else: The band came apart at Broad an hour ago, the tuba first, then the snare, the trumpet still playing its two songs to itself on the way up somebody’s steps. They walked the avenue home with the last of the stragglers, and a few blocks short of Dupre Street, under the oaks, they sat down on the neutral ground, and Lena said she would get up again in a minute.

body: There is one streetlight on this stretch, and it comes down yellow through the live oaks and lands on the wet grass in pieces. The oaks reach clear across the avenue from both sides. In the one over Jack somebody, in some year, threw beads up into the branches, and they hang there in loops, purple and green and gold, a few of them sun-bleached nearly white, one long strand stirring whenever the air does. The grass is soaked. The city is quieter now and not quiet: far off toward the river a band is still going, a trombone and a bass drum and not much else, and every so often down toward Broad somebody leans on a car horn in the rhythm of the Who Dat, a little farther away each time.

Now and then somebody goes by on the far side of the avenue, toward home: two girls in black-and-gold boas carrying their shoes; an old man in a Saints windbreaker walking a bicycle with a crawfish pot bungeed to the rack; a boy of twenty or so with HARTLEY ironed onto the back of a plain gold T-shirt, who stops under the streetlight, raises both fists at the oak, says “Who dat” up into it, conversationally, and walks on.

He has his back against the trunk and the Carhartt spread on the grass under the two of them, and the cold coming up through it. Lena is against his left side with her head on his shoulder. Her hair is down; it gave up on the pencil somewhere around midnight, and it smells of fireworks. What was left of the stranger’s fleur-de-lis has come off her cheekbone onto his shirt, at the shoulder, where her cheek is. Her knees are drawn up, and two fingers of her right hand are hooked into the placket of his shirt, at the second button. His left arm is round her, under her arm, his hand on her ribs.

Laney is asleep against Lena’s other side with her mouth open and somebody’s beads wound twice round her wrist. On the curb a few yards off Theo is awake, sitting with his good coat pulled down round his knees and his chin in the collar, turned sideways to the avenue. On the next bench Kevin sleeps sitting up, chin on his chest, the BlackBerry in one hand and his rosary in the other, and Margot sits beside him, awake, with her notebook shut on her knee and one of Kevin’s beads pinched between her finger and thumb.
“Picture it,” Theo says, to the avenue. “A city of three hundred thousand people, and not one chair.”
“You’re on a curb.”
“A curb isn’t a chair, Costigan. A curb is a *suggestion*.”
“He went under in the fourth decade,” Margot says, low, across the grass. “I’m holding his place.”
“That’s how it starts.”
“I’m a social scientist. I’m holding it *neutrally*.”
Against Lena, Laney says, quite clearly, “Not in those shoes,” and is gone again.
Lena’s fingers tighten in his shirt. Her eyes are shut. “Don’t let me sleep out here,” she says, into his shoulder. “Mama’ll kill you.”
“Me.”
“You. She likes me.”
“She sends me for ice.”
“That’s how you know,” Lena says.
Down at Broad the horn does the chant again, fainter. Lena turns her face a little further in against his shirt, so that the next thing comes out muffled, and he has to put his head down to get it.
“I wanted you here for this,” she says. “Since September.”

Her fingers come loose from the button and don’t close again. Her breathing goes long and slow and even. He looks at the part in her hair under the streetlight, and the bits of gold paint caught in it, and he opens his mouth, and whatever he had to say back to that he keeps, and after a minute she is too far under to hear it anyway.
At 3:44 the RAZR goes off against his thigh, twice.
He works it out of his jeans with his right hand and opens it against his knee, one-handed, on its cracked hinge. The little screen lights his fingers green.

body: He laughs with his mouth shut, and Lena’s head goes up and down on his shoulder with it and doesn’t wake. She sent it with the confetti still coming down in Miami, from a trailer in Burnaby, most likely, in Kyle’s cap and Cassie’s wig, and it has been six hours in the jammed air over this city looking for him. He can see her doing it: both thumbs, the cap on backward over the wig, Kyle from Fort Wayne beside her with his head in his hands. The man on the porch is asleep on Dupre Street by now, or ought to be, in his Brees jersey, with his voice gone.
He answers it. The keys go in one at a time under his thumb, slow, because it’s one hand and T9, and his other arm is still under her.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south. Friday at a truck stop under Picacho Peak she called from Burnaby. Wardrobe took my flannel: Cassie wears it; it got the part. The geese are the size of Labradors. I read her one of Hale’s rude ones at the pump. Saturday night she called again after wrap, and I read her two more, on the Broussards’ front steps. I told Lena’s little sister who she is. My girlfriend. In Canada. She wants a call at the kickoff. Sunday at the kickoff I had the phone open to call her, and it rang in my hand. She was in a trailer in Burnaby in a Colts cap, wearing it into Cassie’s wig. She bought her own *Moviegoer* at the airport and read it on the plane. Being in the movie doesn’t make anything real either, she says. She owes me a picture. She turned her TV off to hear the kickoff on Dupre Street. Her text after the game got to me at a quarter to four in the morning, on Esplanade. She’s taking full credit.

body: When he looks up from the shut phone, Theo is looking at him.

He has turned round on the curb to do it. His face is up in the streetlight, over the collar of the good coat, and it isn’t doing any of the things Theo’s face does for a living. His hands are knotted together round his knees. For as long as it takes the horn at Broad to come round once more, faint, he looks at Jack across the wet grass, and at the top of Lena’s head on Jack’s shoulder.
Theo shuts his eyes.
He keeps them shut. He leans his head back against the pole of a parking sign and sits there with his eyes closed and his face turned up into the light, and says nothing.

A car comes up Esplanade from the river under the oaks, slow, with the light bar on its roof dark. It’s an NOPD cruiser, with a strand of gold beads hung over the side mirror and a paper cup crushed flat under one wiper, and it pulls to the curb by the oak a car length past Theo’s shoes and sits there idling. The driver’s window comes down.

It’s Luc. He has been working the Quarter all night with every other cop in the city, and it is on him: the shirt gone soft at the collar, his eyes red at the rims from a night of Bourbon Street. On his shoulder the radio is going, a dispatcher reading out a string of numbers in a voice as tired as his. He puts his forearm on the window frame. His eyes go over the pile on the grass: Laney with her mouth open; Kevin asleep with his rosary and Margot holding his place on it, who looks right back; Theo, whose eyes are open again. They come to his sister, asleep on Jack’s shoulder, her hand fallen open on his shirt. Then they come up to Jack’s face, and keep at it.
Jack’s left hand is on Luc’s sister’s ribs. He leaves it where it is.
“Get her home before the sun,” Luc says.
“Yes, sir.”

Luc looks at him a little longer, and the window goes back up. The cruiser pulls off the curb and rolls away up Esplanade toward the park, unhurried, under the oaks, until it turns, and the avenue is empty again.
“Was that a threat,” Margot says, “or a blessing.”
“Yes,” Jack says.
On the bench Margot moves Kevin’s bead along by one, and looks at it as though it did that by itself.

body.text: Mémère’s *Attention* is still in his ear. He says a Hail Mary under his breath for the house on Dupre Street and everybody asleep in it.

body: The phone is shut in his right hand. Lena has gone heavy all down his left side, heavier than she was an hour ago, and her hair has come across his chest, and her hand has slid off his shirt onto the Carhartt and lies there palm up. Above them in the oak the beads somebody threw up there in some other year turn on their strands when the air moves, and catch the streetlight, and turn back. He sits under them with the cold coming up through the Carhartt and her breathing against his arm, and looks down the avenue toward the Quarter, where the sky hasn’t started yet. He gives it a little under three hours.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold.
